Extract  from  diary  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy. 

July  1863. — A  beautiful,  still  morning  when  I  left  the  vessel 
before  daybreak  and  pulled  for  the  Weehawhen.  I  p  anchor,  and 
before  sunrise  off  Wagner  with  all  the  ironclads.  Opened  tire,  and 
soon  stopped  the  feeble  reply  it  made.  Could  see  the  new  work  of 
our  troops  thrown  up  last  night.  Pounded  away,  scattering  sand  till 
after  10,  when  a  steamer  was  seen  coming  past  Sumter  with  a  flag  of 
truce.  Ceased  firing  and  responded  with  similar  flag,  for  our  wounded 
were  on  board,  and  there  was  to  be  an  exchange.  Presently  she  came 
quite  close  and  hailed,  stating  the  errand.  1  answered  that  the 
arrangement  was  with  the  army,  w'hich  would  attend  to  them.  So  I 
turned  down  channel  to  my  vessel,  for  the  exchange  of  the  wmunded 
would  occupy  the  day.  Met  a  steamer  from  army  coming  up  with 
their  wounded. 

In  the  afternoon  General  Gillmore  telegraphed  that  his  operation  had 
succeeded,  and  thanked  me  for  the  very  efficient  fire  of  the  vessels. 
In  the  evening  the  enemy  felt  what  the  new  work  might  be,  and 
opened  fire  on  it. 


Order  of  General  Beauregard,  C.  S.  Army,  to  Lieutenant-Colonel  Harris,  C,  S.  Army. 


Headquarters  Department  S.  C.,  Ga,,  and  Fla., 

Charleston ,  S.  C. ,  July  1863. 

Colonel:  Examine  condition  for  resistance  of  Battery  Wagner  and 
report  in  person  as  soon  as  possible.  Explain  to  General  Taliaferro 
that  he  must  fight  the  fleet  with  sand;  that  the  battery  originally  was 
only  meant  to  defend  against  land  approach.  The  battery  must  be 
held  as  long  as  possible;  even  twenty -four  hours  are  important. 

Respectfully,  etc., 

G.  T.  Beauregard, 

General ,  Commanding. 

Lieutenant-Colonel  D.  B.  Harris, 

Chief  Engineer ,  Morr  is  Island. 


Order  of  General  Beauregard,  C.  S.  Army,  to  Brigadier-General  Taliaferro,  C.  S.  Army. 

Headquarters  Department  S.  C.,  Ga.,  and  Fla., 

Charleston ,  S.  C. ,  July  1863. 

General:  The  batteries  designed  to  render  Batteries  Wagner  and 
Gregg  untenable  by  the  enemy,  if  reduced,  not  being  completed,  it  has 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


395 


become  exigent  that  those  last  batteries  should  be  held  to  the  last  extrem¬ 
ity.  Wagner,  being  under  guns  of  Sumter  and  Gregg,  should  be  held 
by  infantry  and  siege  guns  alone  until  its  parapets  and  bombproofs  are 
destroyed  and  no  longer  afford  shelter  against  artillery.  The  general 
regards  it  almost  improbable  that  another  assault  will  be  attempted. 
Furthermore,  the  evacuation  of  Wagner  does  not  necessarily  involve 
immediate  abandonment  of  Gregg,  which,  with  reduced  garrison  and 
sharpshooters  tilling  the  sand  hills  between  it  and  Wagner,  may  be 
held  for  several  days  longer.  When  obliged  to  quit  either  work,  the 
guns  must  be  thoroughly  disabled  by  spiking,  knocking  off  trunnions, 
cutting  and  burning  carriages  and  bombproofs,  and  by  blowing  up  the 
magazines  and  parapets.  In  view  of  the  great  improbability  of  an 
assault,  may  it  not  be  well  to  reduce  the  garrison  minimum  to-morrow 
morning  just  about  2  o’clock. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Thomas  Jordan, 

Chief  of  Staff. 

Brigadier-General  W.  B.  Taliaferro, 

Morris  Island.

Navy  Department,  July  2 f  1863. 

Sir:  Your  No.  13,  dated  the  17th  instant,  has  been  received.  Your 
request  for  a  supply1’  of  coal  and  for  certain  shells  has  received  atten¬ 
tion  by  the  appropriate  bureaus. 

Two  hundred  men  have  been  sent  out  to  you  on  the  U.  S.  S.  Aries 
from  Boston,  60  in  the  Bermuda  from  Philadelphia,  and  200  more  will 
be  sent  soon,  which  are  all  that  can  be  furnished  at  present.  You 
must  use  the  contraband  element,  as  far  as  it  can  be  with  advantage  to 
the  service,  in  supplying  deficiencies  in  the  squadron. 

A  battalion  of  marines  (400)  is  now  being  collected  and  will  be  sent 
down  to  you  soon. 

The  Department  desires  the  Aries  to  be  sent  back  to  Boston  as  soon 
as  she  delivers  her  men. 

I  am,  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Order  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren ,  U.  S.  Nary,  for  the  cooperation 
of  a  howitzer  force  in  the  proposed  attack  upon  Fort  Wagner. 

Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island,  July  25,  1863 — 9:30  p.  m. 

I  am  informed  by  the  general  commanding  ashore  that  an  assault 
on  his  lines  by  the  enemy  is  not  improbable  to-morrow,  and  for  some 
days  at  daybreak,  and  he  has  requested  of  me  the  aid  of  a  howitzer 
force. 

Six  boats  will  be  detailed  for  this  duty,  four  of  which  will  remain 
in  readiness  near  the  advanced  line  all  night;  the  other  two  will  join 
in  season  before  daybreak. 

The  howitzers  will  use  canister  and  will  be  placed  so  as  to  sweep 
the  approach  to  our  lines,  and  will  use  the  utmost  vigilance  in  detect¬ 
ing  any  movement  of  the  enemy. 

The  Weehawken  will  move  in  before  daybreak,  as  near  as  will  be  safe, 
to  avoid  grounding;  guns  loaded  with  canister,  and  prepare  to  open  on 
the  enemy. 

All  the  ironclads  will  be  prepared  to  move,  and  the  first  gun  will  be 
the  signal  for  them  to  attack  the  fort  and  sweep  the  ground  between 
it  and  our  lines,  according  to  the  circumstances. 

The  enemy  must  not  obtain  the  advantage  he  seeks,  nor  attempt  it 
with  impunity. 

I  shall  repair  to  the  spot  at  the  first  notice. 

J.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  the  muster  of  the  army  transport  steamer  Arago  regarding 
the  capture  of  the  steamer  Raima. 

U.  S.  Transport  Arago, 

New  York,  July  26,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  arrival  of  the  steamship  Arago 
in  this  harbor  with  the  prize  steamer  Emma,  of  London,  in  tow,  which 
vessel  1  captured  at  10:30  a.  m.  Friday,  July  24,  in  latitude  33°  41'  N. 
and  longitude  76°  13'  W.,  while  on  my  way  from  Hilton  Head,  S.  C., 
to  this  port. 

I  left  Hilton  Head,  S.  C.,  at  10  a.  m.  Thursday,  July  23,  and  called 
off  Charleston  Bar  at  3:15  p.  m.,  where  I  waited  for  dispatches,  etc., 
from  General  Gillmore  and  Admiral  Dahlgren  until  5  p.  m.,  in  obedi¬ 
ence  to  the  orders  of  Captain  Lamb,  assistant  quartermaster  Depart¬ 
ment  of  the  South.  At  5  p.  m.  I  left  Charleston  Bar  for  this  port,  and 
at  daylight  Friday,  24th,  discovered  a  steamer  with  very  black  smoke 
to  the  northward  and  eastward  of  us,  with  which  we  were  closing  fast. 
At  6:15  a.  m.  we  commenced  to  pass  bales  of  compressed  cotton,  and 
during  the  hour  following  passed  at  least  100  bales. 

At  7:15  a.  m.  we  were  sufficiently  close  to  the  strange  steamer  to  be 
perfects  certain  that  the  cotton  came  from  her.  This  and  otheractions 
fully  disclosed  her  character  as  a  blockade  runner. 

At  7 :30  a.  m. ,  having  consulted  with  General  Truman  Seymour,  U.  S. 
Army,  Captain  Taylor,  U.  S.  Navy,  and  many  other  passengers,  1 
determined  to  give  chase;  altered  my  course  accordingly  and  came  up 
with  her  at  10:  30  a.  m. 

No  name  could  be  discovered  on  the  vessel,  and  the  captain  refused 
to  say  what  vessel  it  was,  from  what  port  or  where  bound;  claimed  to 
be  sailing  wdthout  papers  or  flag,  but  freely  and  at  once  acknowledged 
her  to  be  from  Dixie  or  Southern  States,  and  a  prize.  I  thereupon 
ordered  him  with  her  crew  on  board  of  this  ship,  and  placed  a  prize 
crew  on  board  of  her,  with  my  chief  officer,  Mr.  Mallory,  in  command, 
and  took  her  in  tow.  Subsequently  I  discovered  the  vessel’s  name  to 
be  the  Emma ,  from  Wilmington,  N.  C.,  loaded  with  cotton,  turpentine, 
rosin,  etc.,  and  bound  to  Bermuda.  The  reason  assigned  for  heaving 
the  cotton  overboard  is,  that  from  daylight,  it  was  supposed  this  ship 
was  in  chase,  and  that  by  heaving  it  overboard  it  would  not  only 
lighten  their  vessel  and  increase  her  speed,  but  it  was  hoped  our  atten¬ 
tion  might  be  diverted  by  it,  and  their  chances  of  escape  improved. 

Just  before  we  came  up  with  her,  nearly  everything  about  decks 
was  either  thrown  overboard  or  willfully  destroyed. 

I  have  caused  a  thorough  search  to  be  made  and  inventory  of  furni¬ 
ture.  etc.,  taken,  but  no  papers  of  any  description  have  been  discovered. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  obedient  servant, 

Henry  A.  Gadsden, 

Commander. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy.

Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island,  Judy  27,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  it  in  contemplation  to  withdraw  the  Pawnee  for  a  few 
days  from  Stono  to  assist  operations  here.  When  this  may  be,  will 
depend  upon  circumstances. 

Her  absence  will  be  supplied  by  a  monitor. 

Meanwhile  you  can  prepare  the  vessel  for  work  by  having  sand 
bags  ready  to  pack  about  the  boilers  and  other  dangerously  vulnerable 
parts.  If  possible,  the  upper  spars  should  be  struck. 

As  there  can  be  no  great  sea,  I  wish  to  make  the  broadside  as  heavy 
as  possible— eight  or  ten  guns  on  a  side — IX-inch,  if  the  deck  will  bear 
them.  This  may  be  shored  temporarily. 

In  short,  make  the  best  disposition  for  a  strong  broadside  with  a 
light  draft. 

1  hough  I  need  your  services  in  Stono,  yet  I  shall  be  unwilling  to 
deprive  you  of  the  service  in  view  in’ ease  you  desire  to  remain  with 

the  Pawnee.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U  S. 

Navy ,  regarding  reinforcements  and  measures  for  the  relief  of  those 

serving  on  ironclads. 

Navy  Department,  July  2 8 ,  1863. 

Sir:  Two  hundred  men  have  been  sent  out  to  you  in  the  Aries, 
which  sailed  from  Boston  on  the  25th  instant.  On  her  return  to  New 
York,  to  which  port  you  will  order  her,  200  more  will  be  dispatched 
to  you.  The  Department  desires  you  to  enlist  for  service  in  the 
squadron  as  many  able-bodied  contrabands  as  you  can,  especially  for 
firemen  and  coal  heavers.  There  is  a  great  demand  at  present  from 
all  quarters  for  seamen,  and  the  contraband  element  must  be  used 
where  it  can  with  advantage. 

It  is  considered  important  that  the  officers  as  well  as  the  men  on 
board  the  ironclads  should  be  relieved  from  time  to  time  by  those  on 
board  the  more  comfortable  vessels,  which  will  have,  it  is  thought,  a 
favorable  effect  on  the  health  of  all,  and  especially  upon  those  who 
have  been  employed  for  some  time  in  the  ironclads. 

The  Department  contemplates  procuring  a  large  steamer,  with  ample 
accommodations,  such  as  those  employed  on  Long  Island  Sound,  to  be 
attached  to  your  squadron  for  the  accommodation  of  the  men  of  the 
reserve  force  as  they  are  relieved  from  time  to  time  from  duty  on  the 
ironclads. 

The  U.  S.  steam  sloop  Richmond,  at  present  attached  to  Admiral 
Farragut’s  squadron,  has  been  ordered  to  report  to  you,  unless  her 
services  are  necessary  for  important  operations  in  that  squadion. 

The  Mahaska  and  the  other  double-end  steamers  will  also  soon  join 

''  °Five  thousand  men  have  been  ordered  to  reinforce  General  Gillmore. 

The  battalion  of  marines,  about  400  in  number,  will  leave  New  York 
on  the  steamer  Arago  on  Friday  next,  lhese,  with  the  additional 
seamen  sent,  will,  it  is  hoped,  enable  you  to  carry  out  successfully 
your  plans. 

Very  respectfully,  etc.,  Gideon  \\  elles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Rear-Admiral  Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Port  Royal.

Order  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren ,  IT.  S.  Navy,  to  Commander  Calhoun , 

U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Weehawken,  to  proceed  with  that 

vessel  and  the  Conemaugh  to  Wassaiv  Sound,  in  view  of  an  expected 

attack  from,  the  enemy. 

Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island,  July  28,  1863. 

Sir:  I  am  just  informed  by  General  Gillmore  that  a  deserter  from 
Savannah  reports  that  the  Savannah,  accompanied  by  some  gunboats, 
is  about  to  make  an  attempt  upon  the  Nahant  and  Unadilla ,  now 
blockading  Wassaw  Sound. 

With  every  confidence  in  the  gallantry  of  our  officers  and  men  and 
the  capacity  of  the  vessels,  I  do  not  feel  justified  in  allowing  a  chance 
to  the  enemy. 

Wherefore,  as  General  Gillmore  is  of  the  opinion  that  the  report  of 
the  deserter  is  so  far  not  to  be  disregarded  that  we  should  be  pre¬ 
pared,  1  have  concluded  to  dispatch  your  vessel  in  tow  of  the  Cone¬ 
maugh  to  Wassaw,  when  you  will  report  to  Commander  Downes. 

The  return  of  the  Conemaugh  must  be  controlled  by  circumstances. 
If,  in  the  opinion  of  Commander  Downes,  her  presence  is  not  needed, 
she  will  return  to  this  place. 

With  this  reinforcement  there  can  be  little  doubt  of  the  issue  if  the 
enemy  decide  on  attacking. 

I  have  addressed  this  to  you,  but  it  is  designed  for  the  guidance  of 
all  concerned. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 
Commander  E.  R.  Coliioun, 

Commanding  U  S.  Ironclad  Weehawken. 


Report  of  Captain  Green ,  U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  off  Charleston , 
o.  6.,  regarding  matters  pertaining  to  the  vessels  stationed  there. 

U.  S.  S.  Canandaigua, 

Off  Charleston,  S.  C,  July  28,  1863. 

Sir.  I  have  respectfully  to  state  that  the  Dai  Citing  and  Ottawa 
are  the  only  vesseks  now  employed  on  blockade  service  that  have  a 
sufficiently  light  draft  to  navigate  about  the  Rattlesnake  Shoal,  and 
between  it  and  the  mainland,  and  that  their  commanding  officers  have 
never  had  an  opportunity  of  acquiring  a  knowledge  of  the  navigation 
ot  those  waters.  I  would  therefore  suggest  that  they  may  be  allowed 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


408 


to  devote  a  part  of  a  day  to  steaming’,  sounding,  etc.,  in  that  vicinity, 
in  order  that  they  may  obtain  the  necessary  knowledge  of  the  naviga¬ 
tion  thereabouts  to  enable  them  to  move  promptly  and  with  safety  at 
night. 

The  vessels  on  blockade  service  can  not  be  stationed  in  the  most 
advantageous  manner  without  the  number  to  be  thus  employed  is 
known.  Should  it  be  convenient,  will  you  please  inform  me  of  the 
names  of  the  vessels  now  assigned  to  that  duty,  and  notify  me  before 
night,  daily,  of  the  withdrawal  from  or  detail  of  additional  vessels 
for  it? 

Believing  that  the  blockade  of  this  port  would  be  rendered  the  most 
effective  by  stationing  the  few  vessels  at  my  command  at  anchor,  I 
have  so  disposed  of  them,  with  the  exception  of  one  night,  on  which 
occasion  a  vessel  cruised  in  the  offing.  It  is  not  probable  that  an 
attempt  to  violate  the  blockade  will  be  made  during  the  present  moon¬ 
light  nights,  and  therefore  it  is  my  intention,  unless  you  should  direct 
otherwise,  or  the  number  of  vessels  on  blockade  duty  should  be 
increased,  to  continue  the  anchor  blockade. 

I  beg  leave  to  call  your  attention  to  the  unseaworthy  condition  of 
the  schooner  Norfolk  Packet.  She  was  surveyed  and  condemned  a 
short  time  previous  to  your  assuming  command  of  this  squadron.  She 
has  but  ten  days’  supplies  on  board. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

.1 .  F.  Green, 

Captain  and  Senior  Officer  Preseni. 

Rear-Admiral  John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Abstracting  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Catskill ,  Commander  Badgers,  IT.  S.  Navy. 

July  28,  1863. — At  12  m.  underway  and  engaged  the  enemy.  Ex¬ 
pended  20  Xl-inch  shell  and  12  solid  shot  during  the  action.  At 
2:25  p.  m.  ceased  tiring  and  drew  off  and  anchored. 

July  29. — At  10  a.  m.  the  Ironsides,  Passaic,  and  Patapsco  engaged 
the  enemy.  At  12:15  p.  m.  the  Ironsides  commenced  firing  on  Fort 
Wagner.  At  4  p.  m.  underway  and  proceeded  to  engage  the  enemy. 
At  6:40  hauled  off  and  anchored.  Expended  in  action  28  Xl-inch  shell. 

July  30. — At  8:55  a.  m.  underway  and  standing  up  to  engage  the 
enemy  at  Fort  Wagner.  Expended  in  action  42  Xl-inch  shell  and  5 
Xl-inch  shrapnel.  At  12:24  p.  m.  withdrew  from  action.  At  4:05 
p.  m.  the  Patapsco  got  underway,  and  at  4:20  commenced  firing  at 
Gumming’ s  Point. 

August  1. — Off  Morris  Island.  At  9:45  got  underway  and  steamed 
toward  Wagner.  At  10  opened  fire  on  Fort  Wagner  with  our  Xl-inch 
gun;  distance,  1,600  to  2,000  yards.  At  10:20  came  to  anchor.  At 
11:10  hove  up  anchor.  At  11:20  ceased  firing,  and  at  11:50  came  to 
anchor.  Ammunition  expended,  23  Xl-inch  shell.

Abstract  Jog  of  the  Jr.  8.  8.  New  Ironsides ,  Captain  Rowan ,  U.  8.  Navy. 

July  29,  1863. — Midnight  to  4  a.  m.  Fort  Sumter,  Cumming’s  Point, 
and  dames  Island  shelling  our  troops;  Morris  Island  engaged.  At 
10: 15  the  admiral  made  signal  to  commence  action.  Got  underway 
and  stood  up  the  channel;  came  to  anchor,  Fort  Wagner,  [bearing],  per 
compass,  W.  4  N.,  distant  1,400  yards,  Fort  Sumter  N.  W.  4  N.,  dis¬ 
tant  If  miles.  Meridian  to  4  p.  m. :  Moderate  breeze  from  the  south¬ 
ward  and  clear.  Lying  under  the  guns  of  rebel  batteries  and  Fort 
Sumter.  Monitors  Passaic  and  Montauk  engaging  Fort  Wagner  and 
shelling  the  beach  between  the  batteries  Wagner  and  Gregg.  Owing 
to  the  breeze  from  southward  ship  would  not  swing  to  ebb  tide  and 
the  guns  of  the  port  battery  would  not  bear.  At  12:20,  ship  swing¬ 
ing,  opened  with  starboard  150-pounder  rifle  on  Battery  Gregg.  Com¬ 
menced  working  engines  to  bring  broadside  to  bear.  At  12:  30  opened 
with  starboard  broadside  on  Fort  Wagner.  Also  opened  with  50- 
pounder  rifle  on  spar  deck  on  Sumter.  Continued  tiring  on  Fort 
Wagner  with  good  effect.  Fort  Wagner  replying,  but  Fort  Sumter 
and  Battery  Gregg  firing  briskly,  most  of  the  shots,  however,  passing- 
just  over  the  ship.  During  the  engagement  ship  was  struck  twice, 
once  on  plating  starboard  side,  once  on  deck  forward  the  smokestack 
without  material  damage.  Expended  170  Xl-inch  shell  (10  and  7 
second),  15  150-pounder  rifle  percussion  shell,  25  50-pounder  percus¬ 
sion.  At  2:45  flagship  made  signal,  ceased  firing.  At  2:50  beat 
retreat  and  withdrew  from  action,  giving  Fort  Wagner  two  broadsides 
while  underway.  Experienced  much  difficulty  in  keeping  broadside 
bearing  on  the  fort,  owing  to  strong  breeze  from  the  southward  dur¬ 
ing  the  engagement.  From  4  to  6,  rebel  batteries  firing  on  our  troops. 
At  5  p.  m.  Catskill  and  Montauk  opened  fire  on  Wagner,  shelling  Cum¬ 
ming’s  Point  and  Fort  Wagner.  At  6:  30  Catskill  and  Montauk  ceased 
firing;  batteries  and  our  troops  continued  firing. 

July  30. — From  midnight  to  8  firing  between  our  troops  and  rebel 
batteries.  At  10  a.  m.  cleared  sh^p  for  action.  At  10.40  got  under¬ 
way.  At  11.32  opened  on  Cumming’s  Point  from  port  battery,  the 
enemy  replying  from  Battery  Gregg  and  Fort  Sumter.  From  merid¬ 
ian  to  4:  At  anchor  under  the  guns  of  the  rebel  batteries,  engaging 
Battery  Gregg  with  poll  broadside.  At  12  the  Catskill  withdrew 
from  action.  Firing  at  Battery  Gregg  at  extreme  elevation  on  weather 
roll  with  15-second  fuzes,  with  good  effect,  the  shell  bursting  in  and 
over  the  battery.  Firing  from  150-pounder  rifle  with  percussion  shell, 
the  enemy  firing  slowly  from  Batteiy  Gregg.  At  12:15  fired  spar- 
deck  rifle  at  Fort  Sumter.  At  1:45  steamed  out  of  range.  During 
the  action  expended  329  Xl-inch  shell  and  37  rifle  150-pounder  shell. 
Ship  was  struck  twice.

disabled  rifle  gun.  Fired  twice  from  the  XV-inch  gun,  then  ceased 
firing.  At  1:  30  commenced  firing  XV-inch  gun;  fired  3  times.  At 
3  got  underway  and  steamed  out  of  range.  Fired  from  XV-inch  gun 
one  shot,  12  shells;  rifle  fired  one  shot  and  9  shells. 

August  1.  At  10:  45  p.  m.  beat  to  quarters,  got  underway  in  com¬ 
pany  with  Montauk  and  steamed  up  toward  Fort  Wagner.  A  brisk 
fire  was  going  on  between  our  forces  and  the  rebels.  Secured  every¬ 
thing  for  action,  deck  plates  and  fighting  hatches.  At  11:  20  the  firing 
ceased;  returned  to  our  anchorage.  At  11 :  50  came  to  anchor,  removed 
deck  plates  and  fighting  hatches. 


Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Montauk ,  Commander  Fairfax ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

July  2 9 ,  1863. — At  5:  20  opened  fire  on  Fort  Wagner.  At  6  came  to 
anchor  near  the  Ironsides.  Expended  in  the  action  this  p.  m.  5  XV- 
inch  shells,  19  Xl-inch  shells. 

August  1. — At  4:45  anchored  in  main  Ship  Channel.  Our  forces 
firing  on  the  enemy.  At  10:30  the  enemy  apparently  attacking  in  force. 
Got  underway  and  steamed  to  the  N.  X.  W.  Opened  fire  at  10:  50  p.  m. , 
being  in  position.  Ceased  firing  at  11:  20  and  returned  to  our  former 
anchorage.  Expended  3  Xl-inch  shells. 


Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the  need  of 
steamers  for  towing  the  ironclads. 

No.  42.]  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  July  29,  1863. 

Sir:  The  frequent  calling  for  temporary  presence  of  monitors  at 
different  points  renders  it  important  to  have  one  or  two  side-wheel 
steamers  of  great  power  for  towing,  otherwise  a  vessel  is  taken  from 
the  blockade.  Such  would  also  be  useful  in  communication  between 
this  and  Port  Royal,  where  our  depot  is. 

I  have  concluded  to  cover  the  deck  of  the  monitors  with  sand  bags 
for  action,  and  have  asked  for  a  number  from  the  Bureau  of  Equipment, 
which  I  beg  may  be  forwarded  with  dispatch;  also  a  lot  of  coal  bags;  it 
is  too  rough  at  this  anchorage  to  coal  the  monitors,  etc.,  in  any  other 
way. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  A.  DaTilgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

U.  S.  S.  New  Ironsides, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  July  30 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  the  following  amount  of  damage

Gregg  this  day. 

One  shot  hit  direct  above  No.  6  port,  on  upper  edge  of  iron  plating,

Another  shot  passed  over  from  port  side,  aft  the  turret,  went 
through  main  stanchion,  and  cut  main  rail  in  two.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren ,  U.  _  S.  Navy ,  regarding  general 
matters  pertaining  to  his  command. 

No.  44.]  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Of  Morris  Island ,  July  30 ,  1863. 

Sir:  The  position  of  affairs  is  not  materially  changed  since  the  date 
of  my  last  dispatch  (July  25),  except  that  our  advanced  batteries  (600 
yards  from  Wagner)  are  in  operation  and  will  receive  frequent  addi¬ 
tions  to  its  armament.  I  have  contributed  four  ride  cannon  with  a 
detachment  of  seamen  (say  120),  under  Captain  Parker,  and  will  land 
more  when  I  have  the  men  to  spare. 

Every  day  two  or  three  of  the  ironclads  join  in  and  sweep  the  ground 
between  Wagner  and  Cumin ing’s  Point,  or  else  tire  directly  into  Wag¬ 
ner,  the  only  objection  to  which  is  that  it  is  drawing  largely  on  the 
endurance  of  our  cannon.  However,  I  have  no  doubt  the  Bureau  of 
Ordnance  will  enable  me  to  meet  this  difficulty. 

The  enemy  also  seek  in  every  way  to  distract  our  attention.  The 
nio-ht  before  last  there  was  an  alarm  from  Stono  about  a  ram,  and  last 


410 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON.  _ 


night  a  deserter  to  the  camp  stated  that  the  ironclad  a’t  Savannah  was 
to  move.  I  had  sent  the  Nahant  to  check  this,  but  as  the  rumor 
added  several  gunboats,  and  the  Bnadllla  alone  was  with  the  Nahant, 
it  seemed  better  to  make  sure,  so  I  sent  down  the  Weehawken  in  tow 
of  the  Conemamgh. 

The  turrets  received  a  shot  occasionally  with  the  usual  result,  and 
the  Ironsides  has  been  struck  repeatedly  by  X-inch  shot  (1,200  to  1,400 
yards)  without  material  impression.  A  shot  from  Fort  Sumter  in 
passing  the  spar  deck  glanced  from  the  edge  of  it  and  by  the  concus¬ 
sion  damaged  the  beam  below,  with  knees  connecting.  If  the  depth  of 
water  would  only  permit  her  to  approach,  I  would  sweep  the  ground 
clean  with  her  powerful  broadside. 

It  is  to  be  remembered  that  Wagner  is  the  key  to  Sumter,  where¬ 
fore  the  enemy  will  spare  no  effort  for  the  defense,  and  will  protract 
any  result  to  the  last. 

There  are  many  little  things  that  would  aid  me  here.  For  instance, 
the  electric  light  which  Professor  Way  exhibited  here,  and  which 
Professor  Henry  (Smithsonian  Institution)  knows  of;  it  would  either 
illuminate  at  night,  if  needed,  or  would  serve  to  signal,  the  eclipse  of 
its  flame  being  perfect;  then  some  small  iron  boats  for  one  or  two  men 
to  scout  at  night. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Oomdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington ,  D.  C.

Order  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Captain  Green , 
U.  S.  Navy,  senior  officer  off  Charleston ,  S.  C.,  enjoining  vigilance  in 
view  of  the  expected  appearance  of  the  Confederate  steamer  Sumter. 

Flag  Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Of  Morris  Island,  July  30,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  20th  instant  your  attention  was  called  to  the  fact  that 
the  Sumter  might  soon  be  expected  on  our  coast,  with  intent  to  pass 
our  blockade. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


411 


The  Navy  Department  has  just  furnished  me  with  an  additional  list 
of  vessels  which  are  reported  to  have  a  similar  errand  in  view. 

The  greatest  vigilance  will  therefore  be  exercised,  and  if  the  least 
attempt  is  made  to  escape  by  any  vessel  which  is  overhauled,  fire  is  to 
be  opened  on  her  until  she  is  completely  disabled. ' 

Pursuit  is  also  to  be  maintained  along  the  channels;  the,  forts  will 
hardly  fire  on  blockade  runners;  and  if  they  do,  it  is  not  likely  to  do 
much  harm  by  night. 

In  the  case  of  the  Sumter ,  she  is  to  be  pursued  even  into  the  harbor, 
at  all  risks,  by  day  or  night,  and  destroyed. 

It  appears  to  me,  also,  that  on  many  occasions  a  boat  or  two  from 
each  vessel  might  scout  the  channels,  and  by  a  shot  or  two  give  notice 
to  our  own  vessels  of  steamers  attempting  to  pass  in. 

Respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Captain  .Joseph  F.  Green, 

Senior  Officer  Present ,  off  Charleston ,  S.  C.

Report  of  Acting  Master  Polleys,  IT.  S.  Navy,  commanding  IT  S.  S. 

Madgie ,  regarding  the  impaired  condition  of  that  vessel. 

U.  S.  S.  Madgie, 

St.  Catherine! s  Sound ,  Georgia ,  August  1 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  to  you  the  following  report  in  regard 
to  the  condition  of  this  ship: 

When  I  joined  her  some  two  months  since  she  was  leaking  at  the 
rate  of  2  inches  per  hour  in  smooth  water;  in  a  seaway,  much  more. 
The  leak  has  steadily  increased  till  at  present  she  leaks  from  4  to  6 
inches.  On  the  26th  instant  I  received  permission  to  examine  her 
bottom  from  Lieutenant  Kittredge,  senior  officer  present.  On  the 
morning  of  the  28th  I  put  her  on  the  beach,  with  tackles  at  the  mast¬ 
head  to  keep  her  upright,  so  that  1  could  examine  the  offshore  side  and 
then  list  her  over  to  examine  the  inshore  side.  On  the  starboard  or 
offshore  side  I  found  about  twenty  or  thirty  sheets  of  copper  off  that 
had  probably  been  off  since  she  was  ashore  on  Cape  Lookout  some 
sixteen  months  since.  She  has  so  flat  a  floor  that  we  could  not  well 
get  at  it,  but  by  cleaning  the  grass  off  with  brooms  we  found  that 
where  the  copper  was  off  her  bottom  was  a  perfect  honeycomb,  it  is 
so  badly  eaten  by  the  worms.  I  send  you  a  sample  of  her  bottom 
planking  and  keel  enclosed  in  a  box.  She  has  no  shoe  on  and  no  cop¬ 
per  on  the  bottom  of  her  keel  that  we  could  see.  On  the  port  side  the 
copper  was  not  off  so  bad,  but  where  it  was  off  is  badly  worm-eaten; 
in  one  place  clear  through  to  the  timbers,  leaving  a  hole  4  inches 
square,  over  which  I  put  a  patch  of  board  and  canvas.  It  is  astonish¬ 
ing  to  me  how  she  has  kept  afloat  so  long.  In  all  my  experience  of 
twenty-five  years  at  sea  I  have  not  seen  a  vessel’s  bottom  in  so  bad 
a  condition.  When  we  heeled  her  offshore  the  water  came  out  of  her 
bottom  like  out  of  a  sieve.  The  iron  extension  that  the  rudder  is 
shipped  on  is  only  held  by  one  bolt,  the  others  having  rusted  off. 
Otherwise  she  is  in  good  condition  as  regards  sails,  rigging,  anchors, 
chains,  etc.,  with  a  good  and  efficient  battery.  I  don’t  think  she  is 
safe  to  go  to  Port  Royal  without  a  tug  in  company.  We  have  only 
the  deck  pumps  to  keep  her  free,  as  the  donkey  pump  has  given  out 
and  the  engineer  reports  he  is  not  able  to  repair  it,  and  her  engine  is 
so  bad  that  she  will  not  steam  ahead  in  a  head  sea  and  will  onlv  go  3 
knots  in  still  water.

tow  of  army  steamer  Peabody ,  with  2,130  barrels  of  powder  and  500

The  bark  struck  on  the  shoals  off  Cape  Lookout,  and  put  into

quartermaster  sent  to  have  the  Peabody >  discharged  and  last  night  700 
barrels  were  put  back  into  the  bark  again  and  the  Peabody  went  to  sea 
with  the  rest. 

I  enclose  a  copy  of  the  invoice  of  the  bark.  Whether  any  of  her 
shell  are  damaged  by  water  1  do  not  know.  The  captain  did  not  say 
that  any  of  them  were  damaged.  In  smooth  water  he  says  that  his 
leakage  is  trifling. 

The  I)ai  Citing's  channels  are  to  be  repaired  to  make  her  masts 
secure,  which  Mr.  Small  says  he  can  complete  by  W ednesday  morning-. 

Perhaps  the  Aries  could  supply  her  place  until  then. 

Mr.  Danby  reports  that  he  hopes  to  have  the  Wissahickon  ready,  if 
all  goes  well  in  shrinking  on  the  band,  by  Wednesday  evening. 

The  Chippewa  has  gone  to  Calibogue  to-day  and  will  be  at  anchor 
in  that  sound  to-night,  where  she  will  be  as  efficient  protection  to 
Hilton  Head  as  if  anchored  over  there,  if  not  more  so.  The  Mercedita 
will  be  at  anchor  at  Hilton  Head,  and  thus  far  that  shore  has  never 
been  without- one  or  more  vessels. 

The  Nahant  and  Cimarron  have  just  arrived. 

The  Prometheus  has  also  arrived  with  the  little  coal  schooner  in  tow. 
She  has  coal  enough  left  to  take  her  to  Charleston  and  back.  I  have 
commenced  to  put  coal  in  coal  schooner  to  send  to  Madgie  and  Stettin 
to-morrow.  The  Powhatan  came  in  with  Cimarron  just  before  sun¬ 
set  and  will  go  to  sea  to-night  if  she  can  get  a  pilot. 

Nahant  came  up  all  the  way  without  a  tow.  Commander  Downes 
does  not  find  her  speed  increased  much.  She  made  3i  knots  coming. 
The  divers  have  not  yet  finished  with  her. 

At  8  p.  m.  the  ordnance  schooner  Mary  K.  Smith  is  just  ready  to 
go  out  in  tow  of  Fair  Ilaven ,  who  thinks  he  will  try  to  get  out  to-night.

Sir:  I  Jiave  the  honor  to  acknowledge  the  receipt  of  your  commu¬ 
nication  of  the  30th  ultimo,  relating  to  the  blockade  of  this  port, 
accompanied  with  a  list  of  and  extracts  referring  to  vessels  reported 
to  be  in  readiness  and  in  course  of  preparation  to  violate  this  blockade; 
and  to  inform  you  that  a  copy  of  your  communication,  and  also  of 
that  of  the  21st  ultimo,  respecting  the  “ Sumter ,  etc.,”  have  been 
forwarded  to  each  of  the  commanding  officers  of  vessels  emploj^ed 
outside  on  the  blockade. 

I  beg  leave  to  remark  that  there  are  but  two  vessels,  viz,  the  Marble¬ 
head  and  Ottawa ,  now  detailed  for  blockade  service  outside  whose 
draft  will  admit  of  their  chasing  inside  the  harbor,  and  that  more 
vessels  of  this  draft  will  be  needed  on  the  approaching  dark  nights. 

There  were  indications  last  night  of  something  attempting  to  come 
out,  but  the  short  period  of  darkness  probably  prevented  it,  if  the 
attempt  was  made. 

Picket  boats  have  been  occasionally  sent  from  the  ships  at  night, 
but  as  they  have  no  refuge  in  squally  or  bad  weather  excepting  our 
own  vessels,  it  has  not  generally  been  practiced. 

The  crews  of  the  Housatonic  and  this  ship  are  so  much  reduced  by 
deficiency  of  complement,  sick,  and  boats’  crews  sent  inside  on  duty 
nightly,  that  1  do  not  think  it  prudent  to  reduce  them  any  further  if 
it  can  be  avoided.  *  *  * 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  F.  Green,

Report  of  Commander  Raich,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U  S.  S. 

Pawnee,  regarding  the  readiness  of  that  vessel  for  special  service  off 

Morris  Island ,  South  Carolina. 

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Pawnee, 

Stono  Inlet,  South  Carolina,  August  f  1863. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  the  Pawnee,  under  my 
command,  is  now  ready  for  the  service  for  which  you  directed  her  to 
be  prepared. 

1  can  bring  nine  broadside  guns  to  bear,  viz,  8  IX-inch  Dahlgren 
guns,  1  100-pounder  Parrott  rifle,  and  by  resorting  to  the  expedient  of 
coming-up  the  mizzen  rigging  I  can  add  the  50-pounder  Dahlgren  rifle, 
thus  making  ten  guns  in  broadside,  which  includes  my  whole  battery. 

Your  order  of  the  27th  ultimo  implies  the  necessity  for  a  light  draft 
with  a  heavy  broadside,  and  I  have  thought  it  proper  to  report  the 
arrangement  as  now  made  'and  take  your  orders  as  to  whether  1  shall 
add  the  50-pounder  Dahlgren  rifle  to  the  nine  broadside  gains  alreadv 
fitted.  s  J 

I  deem  it  proper  to  report  that  there  will  be  some  disadvantages  in 
adding  the  tenth  gun  to  the  broadside,  prominent  among  which  are  an 
increased  draft  of  water  aft  and  an  increased  sluggishness  in  the  action 
of  the  helm.  To  this  we  have  attributed  the  difficulty  of  steering  the 
Pawnee,  and  especially  has  this  difficulty  been  felt  since  1  placed  some 
270  fathoms  of  chain  cable  as  a  protection  to  our  boilers  and  machinery 
abaft  the  center. 

Lhe  following  was  the  ship’s  draft  before  transporting  the  guns: 
Forward,  8  feet  8  inches,  aft,  11  feet  2  inches;  difference,  2  feet  6 
inches.  After  transporting  the  guns:  Forward,  8  feet  4  inches;  aft, 
11  feet  6  inches;  difference,  3  feet  2  inches.  List,  by  having1  nine 
guns  m  broadside,  12  inches. 

1  beg  leave,  respectfully,  to  add  that  I  have  not  filled  any  sand  bags 
the  reason  that  I  was  anxious  not  to  increase  the  ship’s  draft  till 
she  had  passed  the  bar.  I  shall  have  to  run  the  guns  forward  when 
it  becomes  necessary  to  do  so.  I  learned  from  your  chief  of  staff  that 
1  could  get  sand  bags  filled  off  Morris  Island.

Order  of  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren ,  TJ.  S. 
Navy ,  transmitting  memorandum  from  the  Bureau  of  Medicine  and 
Surgery ,  regarding  issue  of  whisky. 


Navy  Department,  August  5,  1863. 

Sir  :  The  Department  regrets  that  it  should  have  been  considered 
necessary,  as  stated  in  one  of  your  dispatches,  to  allow  the  men  whisk}^ 
whilst  under  action.  I  enclose  herewith  a  memorandum  from  the 
Chief  of  the  Bureau  of  Medicine  and  Surgery  on  the  subject.  The 
Department  approves  of  the  views  therein  expressed,  and  desires  that 
they  may  be  carried  out  as  far  as  practicable.  A  ship  load  of  ice  will 
be  sent  out  to  you. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Rear-Admiral  Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Comely.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron,  Port  Royal,  S.  C. 

[Enclosure.] 


[Navy  Department,] 

Bureau  of  Medicine  and  Surgery,  August  f  1863. 

I  am  of  opinion  the  issue  of  whisky  to  men  under  the  circumstances 
mentioned  by  Fleet  Surgeon  Clymer  is  neither  wise  nor  conducive  to 
anything  more  than  a  merely  temporary  result  of  no  beneficial  char- 
acter,  though  I  dissent  with  diffidence  from  so  judicious  and  intelligent 
an  officer.  & 


1  he  issue  of  whisky  to  men  exhausted  by  labor  and  heat  proves  a 
momentary  comfort,  and  stimulates,  it  is  true,  but  the  depression  soon 
recurs  to  make  its  repetition  necessary.  Whisky  is  a  simple  stimulant, 
and  nothing  more.  It  appears  to  me  a  judicious  plan  to  follow  in  the 
fleet  operating  before  Charleston  would  be  as  follows : 

When  the  men  are  turned  out  in  the  morning,  let  them  go  into  the 
water;  immediately  on  coming  out,  issue  a  draft  of  strong  coffee; 
bleak  last  at  the  usual  hour,  with  coffee;  dinner  at  the  usual  hour 
;:;h^CO  e^  1<Ljec!  ;!nd  sweetened  or  tea,  prepared  in  like  manner,  may 
be  served  for  drink  Supper,  if  possible  in  these  long  days,  at  a  later 
houi .  As  it  is  understood  the  Department  proposes  to  supply  ice 
liberally,  tea  or  coffee  of  good  strength,  and  iced,  might  be  allowed  as 
a  common  drink  for  the  men  A  bath  lief  ore  turning  in  at  night  might 
pioie  lefreshing  and  aid  the  sailor  to  recover  his  energies  by  sound 
sleep.  Liquor  should  only  be  served  out  in  special  cases,  when  the 
judgment  of  the  medical  officer  suggests  its  use. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


419 


Oatmeal  mixed  with  water  is  familiar  to  seagoing  men  and  engineers 
as  a  means  of  assuaging  or  diminishing  thirst.  The  step’s  decks  should 
be  kept  as  dry  as  possible,  that  the  sailor,  in  profuse  perspiration  from 
hard  work,  should  have  a  place  to  rest  himself,  where  he  would  not  be 
exposed  to  rheumatism  or  cold. 

Frequent  changes  of  clothing  would  conduce  as  much  to  the  comfort 
of  sailors  in  hot  weather  as  £hey  do  to  all  persons. 

W.  Whelan, 

Chief  of  Bureau.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  measures 
of  protection  in  vie'w  of  expected  movements  of  blockade  runners 
and  the  equipment  of  the  Laird  ram. 

No.  58.]  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  August  5 ,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  received  the  extracts  from  consular  dispatches,  forwarded 
by  the  Department  July  20. 

~  It  is  not  probable  that  many  of  the  vessels  therein  named  will  suc¬ 
ceed  in  reaching  Charleston.  My  attention  was  principally  drawn  to 
the  notice  that  a  ram,  building  at  Lairds’,  was  launched  on  the  4th 
July  at  Liverpool,  and  at  once  transferred  to  dock  for  equipment, 
which,  I  observe  from  other  quarters,  is  progressing  rapidly.  As  this 
violation  of  all  good  faith  may  have  some  influence  on  this  blockade,  I 
hope  the  Department  will  be  able  to  send  here  very  soon  the  Puritan 
or  Dictator ,  either  of  which  will  neutralize  the  expectations  of  the 

enemy.  _ 

In  case  neither  vessel  can  be  read}?-  in  season,  the  probable  effect  of 
a  hostile  ram  on  the  blockade  here  can  be  only  to  interfere  with  our 
supplies;  the  outer  vessels  will  be  driven  off,  but  the  interior  blockade 
could  be  maintained  and  our  operations  proceed,  provided  there  were  a 
sufficient  stock  of  provisions  and  coal  on  hand  for  the  sea  and  land 
forces.  I  would  therefore  recommend: 

First.  That  measures  be  taken  to  forward  a  large  quantity  of  coal, 
rations,  ammunition,  etc.,  which  can  be  landed  on  Folly  and  Morris 
islands,  so  as  to  be  independent  even  of  Port  Royal. 

Second.  That  this  be  proceeded  with  at  once,  and  completed  in  the 
next  thirty  days. 

Port  Royal,  having  a  full  depth  of  water,  may  be  more  difficult  to 
secure,  but  is  by  no  means  impossible  of  maintenance  with  a  resolute 
garrison,  two  or  three  ironclads,  and  some  obstructions  in  the  channel. 

As  the  enemy  would,  no  doubt,  collect  his  cruisers  about  this  ram, 
it  may  be  that  the  isolated  vessels  at  other  points  will  be  driven  off. 
Still,  in  this  way,  I  think  that  the  blockade  of  the  harbor  could  be 
maintained  within,  and  the  operations  against  Charleston  carried  to  a 

conclusion.  ,  ,  , 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren,

Order  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy,  enjoining  vigilance 
against  surprise  from  the  enemy. 

Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island,  August  5, 1863. 

It  is  rumored  that  the  enemy  have  a  ram  near  Fort  Johnson  and 
have  removed  a  line  of  buoys  in  the  harbor.  Whether  the  suspicion 
be  correct  or  not,  it  is  proper  to  guard  against  any  surprise. 

Therefore  the  utmost  vigilance  must  be  used  to  detect  any  move¬ 
ment  and  the  vessels  kept  ready  for  attack  at  the  first  notice  of  the 
enemy’s  approach. 

The  advance  monitor  should  be  underway  or  ready  to  slip  and  the 
picket  boats  feel  well  around  so  as  to  detect  the  least  move. 

J.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren ,  U  S.  Wavy,  requesting  the  restric¬ 
tion  of  foreign  vessels  of  war  from  access  to  Confederate  points. 

No.  61.1  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  August  5,  1863. 

Sir:  To-day  the  British  steamer  Plover  appeared  off  this  port,  and 
the  commander  expressed  to  me  his  wish  to  send  a  boat  to  the  city.  1 
returned  the  reply  that  I  should  offer  no  objection. 

The  occasion  seems  opportune  for  asking  your  attention  to  the  sub¬ 
ject.  In  general,  it  is  the  practice  for  national  vessels  to  pass  an 
ordinary  blockade,  and  until  very  recently  this  was  the  condition  of 
affairs  here.  But  active  operations  are  now  in  progress  against  the 
defenses  of  Charleston,  and  it  seems  to  be  entirely  inadmissible  that 
neutral  parties  should  be  permitted  to  pass  within  the  limits  of  those 

operations.  _  . 

Much  may  be  disclosed  that  will  be  of  material  service  to  the 
enemy,  and  neutral  convenience  should  therefore  give  way  to  the  bel¬ 
li  o-erent  right.  1  do  uot  mean  to  charge  that  officers  of  a  foreign  flag 
wouid  commit  such  an  infraction  of  right  as  to  convey  information, 
but  there  may  be  individuals  in  any  vessel  who  might  not  be  sufficiently 

careful  or  scrupulous.  ... 

It  would  on  all  accounts  be  advisable  that  under  existing  circum¬ 
stances  no  vessels  of  war  should  be  allowed  to  pass  our  lines  at  this 

*  1  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy. 

No  64- 1  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island,  August  8,  1863. 

Sir:  On  the  night  of  the  5th  one  of  the  launches  designed  to  guard 
the  right  flank  of  our  shore  batteries,  having  been  drawn  out  into  the 


422  SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING-  SQUADRON. 

% 

harbor  in  observation  of  a  rebel  steamer,  was  sudden'ly  attacked  by  the 
latter.  Eight  of  the  crew  were  picked  up  and  stated  that  the  launch 
had  been  sunk. 

Yesterday  a  flag  of  truce  came  out  from  the  enemy  with  a  commu¬ 
nication  for  General  Gillmore.  Captain  [J.  F.]  Green,  the  senior  offi¬ 
cer  outside,  reports  to  me  that  the  officer  informed  our  boat  that  the 
launch  had  not  been  sunk,  but  was  captured,  with  Acting  Master 
Haines  and  12  men. 

This  leaves  only  two  men  missing.  The  eight  men  who  were  received 
by  our  boat  were  all  positive  that  they  were  tired  at  from  the  steamer 
when  they  were  in  the  water,  and  as  this  was  in  violation  of  the  usages, 
of  war,  I  addressed  a  communication  to  General  Beauregard  on  the 
subject,  requiring  that  whoever  should  be  convicted  of  the  fact  should 
be  punished,  otherwise  I  would  not  be  able  to  prevent  retaliation  by 
our  men.  As  yet,  1  have  received  no  answer. 

Ensign  B.  H.  Porter  deserves  mention  from  me  for  the  energy, 
courage,  and  intelligence  with  which  he  performed  the  duty  assigned 
him  of  observing  the  enemy,  and  also  for  picking  up  the  eight  men 
who  had  got  out  of  the  launch  in  some  way. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Recur- Admiral.,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles,

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Williams,  IJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Powhatan. 

U.  S.  S.  Powhatan, 

Off  Charleston,  S.  G. ,  August  7, 1863. 

Sir:  1  regret  to  report  that  yesterday  morning,  on  my  arrival  from 
Port  Royal ,  I  was  informed  that  Acting  Master  Edward  L.  Haines,  of 
this  ship,  was  missing,  the  boat  he  was  in  charge  of  having  been  run 
down  the  previous  night  by  a  rebel  steamer,  and  that  in  all  probability 
he  had  been  either  killed  by  the  enemy’s  tire  or  drowned. 

The  only  information  of  the  affair  which  I  have  has  been  gathered 
from  the  crew  of  this  ship’s  launch,  which  boat  Mr.  Haines  had  charge 
of,  but  exchanged  with  Master’s  Mate  Howland,  and  took  the  Wabash's 
boat,  for  the  purpose  of  pulling  farther  up  the  harbor  to  reconnoiter. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

E.  P.  Williams,

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Carpenter,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Catskill. 

U.  S.  Ironclad  Catskill, 

Off  Morr  is  Island,  August  9,  1863. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  of  August  3,  I  have  to  state  that  after 
dark  on  the  evening  of  August  5,  I  anchored  abreast  of  Fort  Wagner 
and  sent  out  the  tug  and  four  picket  boats,  the  tug  to  lay  200  oi” 300 
yards  above  me  betwedh  the  Moultrie  House  and  Fort  Sumter,  two 
picket  boats  in  charge  of  Master  Hogue  to  keep  in  sight  and  close  to 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


423 


her,  and  the  other  2  inshore  between  Wagner  and  our  batteries.  A 
boat  which  came  up  from  the  Ironside s  with  Ensign  Porter  went  to 
Cumming’s  Point,  and  about  10  o’clock  signalized  that  a  steamer  was 
coming  out.  1  went  to  quarters,  hove  up  ni3r  anchor,  and  remained  so 
nearly  an  hour,  but  could  see  nothing;  went  around  the  tug  and  saw 
that  the  boats  were  near  her,  and  then  went  ahead  of  the  tug  and 
anchored  again.  Ensign  Porter,  who  was  at  the  upper  picket  boat, 
came  on  board  and  reported  this  steamer,  describing  her,  and  that  she 
was  lying  under  Sullivan’s  Island,  but  as  the  moon  was  up,  thought 
she  could  not  possibly  get  out  without  being  seen.  He  then  left,  to 
return  to  Cumming’s  Point,  with  orders  to  tell  the  tug  to  lay  more 
astern  of  me,  when  1  saw  a  dark  object  go  rapidly  past  her,  and  some 
distance  inshore,  which  I  knew  must  be  a  steamer.  Went  to  quarters, 
hove  up  my  anchor,  hailed  the  tug,  and  told  her  to  get  out  of  my  line 
of  fire;  made  signals  to  the  boats  to  come  alongside.  As  they  made 
no  alarm  signal,  fired  a  shell  at  the  steamer,  fearing  that  it  might  be 
dangerous  to  our  own  boats,  but  I  then  saw  her  turn  and  go  toward 
the  Moultrie  House  light;  then  fired  a  second  time  just  as  my  anchor 
was  up,  after  which  1  lost  sight  of  her.  Drifted  up  with  a  strong 
flood  tide,  I  should  think,  near  the  block  buoy,  or  three-fourths  of  a 
mile.  Sent  the  tug  in  direction  of  the  boats,  with  orders  to  return 
with  them  as  soon  as  she  found  them,  as  my  pilot  said  we  could  not 
with  safety  go  over  there,  being  on  the  shoal  in  Swash  Channel.  In  a- 
short  time  the  tug  returned  with  Ensign  Porter  and  one  launch, 
reporting  that  the  other  had  been  run  down;  that  he  had  picked  up  8 
men,  pulled  about  there  for  twenty  minutes,  and  that  there  were  no 
more  of  her  crew  about  there.  I  then  concluded  it  best  to  send  the 
tug  to  report  the  circumstances  to  you  and  steam  down  to  my  previ¬ 
ous  anchorage,  which  I  did.  Everything  remaining  quiet,  at  daylight 
I  returned. 

Yerv  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

C.  C.  Carpenter, 

Lieutenant-  Commander ,  Commanding  C 'at shill. 

Rear-Admiral  J.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  General  Beauregard,  C.  S.  Army, 
regarding  an  alleged  violation  of  the  usages  of  war. 

Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  August  6,  1863. 

Sir:  Last  night  one  of  your  steamers  succeeded  in  running  down  a 
boat  of  this  squadron,  and  it  is  stated  by  several  of  our  men  that  they 
were  fired  at  in  the  water  after  the  steamer  had  passed  over  the  boat. 
Of  course  it  was  obvious  to  everyone  that  under  the  circumstances  our 
men  were  entirely  helpless.  ,  .  ...  , 

Such  a  practice  is  entirely  in  violation  of  every  rule  of  civilized 
war  and  I  call  upon  you  to  punish  whoever  can  be  convicted  of  hav¬ 
ing  perpetrated  such  an  act,  otherwise  it  will  be  impossible  for  me  to 
prevent  retaliation  by  our  men  whenever  the  opportunity  may  occur. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Generel  G.  T.  Beauregard, 

Commanding  Confederate  Forces ,  Charleston ,  S.  6.

Extract  from  report  of  Acting  Master  Haines,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 


Philadelphia,  October  % 9 ,  1861/.. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  on  the  5th  of  August,  1863,  the 
U.  S.  steam  sloop  Powhatan ,  Lieutenant-Commander  E.  P.  Williams, 
commanding,  left  her  station  off  Charleston,  S.  C.,  and  pioceeded  to 
Port  Royal,  S.  C. ,  leaving  me  with  the  fleet  in  charge  of  her  first  launch 
and  a  crew  of  24  men,  armed  with  small  arms,  the  launch  having  a  12- 
pound  howitzer;  I  was  assisted  by  Master’s  Mate  Charles  [H-]  How  land, 
of  same  ship.  My  orders  were  to  proceed  on  board  of  U .  S.  S.  Canandm- 
ywaand  remain  until  dark,  then  to  take  my  station  inside  the  bar  as.  a 
picket  boat.  At  5  o’clock  p.  m.  I  left  the  Canandaigua  and  was  taken  in 
tow  by  U.  S.  steam  tug  Rescue,  as  was  also  one  of  the  launches  of  U.  b.  S. 
Housatonic.  We  went  alongside  of  U.  S.  S.  Wabash  and  took  m  tow 
her  first  and  second  launches,  they  being  armed  similar  to  my  own 
launch.  The  Wabash’s  launches  were  commanded  by  an  acting  master  s 
mate,  and  he  remained  in  her  second  launch.  I,  being  senior  officer, 
took  command  of  the  Wabash’s  first  launch,  leaving  Master’s  Mate  How¬ 
land  in  command  of  the  Powhatan s  launch.  .  , , 

Before  taking  my  station,  I  reported  to  Rear-Admiral  J  A.  Dahlgren. 
He  ordered  me  to  report  to  the  officer  commanding  the  U.  b..  monitor 
Catskill ,  she  being  the  guard  ship  for  that  night.  The  admiral  informed 
me  that  two  or  three  of  the  enemy’s  steamers  were  in  the  habit  of 
coming  down  to  Cumming’s  Point  every  night,  and  if  they  came  within 
range,  to  fire  upon  and  sink  them  if  possible,  and  that  Ensign  B.  H. 
Porter  would  be  out  in  a  small  boat,  and  to  be  careful  not  to  fire  at 


In  reporting  to  commander  of  U.  S.  S.  Catskill  (monitor)  he  oideied 
me  to  pull  a  short  distance  above  her,  toward  Fort  Sumter,  and  anchor 
the  launches  under  my  command  in  line,  and  in  sight  of  each  other, 
and  signalize  by  firing  and  displaying  lights  any  danger  that  might 
occur.  ^  I  took  the  lead  of  the  line  toward  the  fort  as  my  station  About 
11  o’clock  p.  m.  Ensign  Porter  came  alongside  and  reported  that  a 
steamer  had  come  down  to  Cumming’s  Point  and  was  now  lying  c  osern, 
and  that  he  thought  she  was  a  blockade  runner.  Leaving  me  he  pulled 
for  the  Catskill,  I  immediately  got  my  anchor  and  let  my  launch  drop 
up  toward  Cumming’s  Point,  in  order  to  get  a  view  of  the  reported 
steamer.  Soon  after  getting  underway  I  made  out  a  steamer  standing 
down  the  channel  dole  to  Morris  Island.  I  immediately  opened  fire 
on  her  from  my  howitzer,  and  made  signals  as  agreed  upon  to  the 
fleet,  at  the  same  time  pulled  my  boat  toward  shoal  water  to  avoi 
colliding  with  her.  Finding  I  could  not  escape,  I  determined  to  boaid 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


426 


and  try  to  take  her,  at  the  same  time  expecting  answers  from  the  other 
launches,  or  Oatshill ,  they  being  in  sight.  I  succeeded  in  boarding, 
her  under  a  heavy  fire  of  musketry.  After  a  short  resistance  we 
were  compelled  by  the  superior  numbers  of  the  enemy  to^  surrender. 
She  proved  to  he  the  C.  S.  S.  Juno ,  manned  by  a  crew  of  50  men,  and 
protected  outside  and  in  by  cotton  bales.  She  also  had  a  torpedo  pro¬ 
jecting  from  her  bow  for  the  purpose  of  blowing  up  any  vessel  she 
might  strike.  She  immediately  returned  to  Charleston  Harbor,  with 
my  launch  in  tow,  much  injured  from  the  collision,  and  transferred  us 
to  C.  S.  ironclad  Chicora ,  Captain  Tucker,  commanding.  On  the 
following  afternoon  we  were  sent  to  Charleston  jail,  where  I  found  two 
of  my  boat’s  crew  who  were  knocked  overboard  from  the  Juno ,  and 
swam  to  Sullivan’s  Island,  where  they  were  taken  prisoners.  x'  * 

On  10th  of  August,  1863,  from  Charleston  we  were  sent  to  Columbia, 
S.  C.  (excepting  Seaman  Amos  A.  Kane,  who  was  retained  in  Charles¬ 
ton  by  the  Confederate  authorites).  *  *  * 

On  the  loth  of  August  we  were  sent  to  Richmond.  My  men  were 
confined  on  Belle  Isle,  near  Richmond,  Va.,  and  I  was  sent  to  Libby 
prison  (the  man  Kane  arriving  in  Richmond,  Va.,  about  loth  Septem¬ 
ber,  1863).  About  the  30th  of  September  1  learned  that  my  men  were 
all  exchanged,  except  Seaman  E.  R.  Clark,  who  died  while  a  prisoner 
on  Belle  Island  [Islej,  near  Richmond,  Va.  *  *  * 

On  the  7th  of  May,  1864,  I  was  sent,  to  Macon,  Ga.,  where  we  were 
confined  in  an  open  stockade  without  shelter  until  we  built  sheds  our¬ 
selves,  after  several  supplications  for  the  materials  *  *  * 

On  the  28th  of  July  I  was  sent  from  Macon  to  Charleston,  S.  C. , 
with  first  600  officers,  for  the  purpose  of  placing  us  under  fire.  On 
arriving  in  Charleston  we  were  confined  in  the  jail  yard;  part  of  the 
officers  were  without  shelter  of  any  kind.  From  the  jail  yard  we 
were  sent  to  a  dirty,  filthy  work-house,  infested  with  all  manner  of 
vermin,  and  the  only  means  whereby  we  could  escape  these  torments 
was  to  give  our  parole,  which  resulted  in  a  change  of  quarters  to  the 
Roper  Hospital,  a  very  comfortable  building.  *  *  *  On  30th  of 

September,  1864,  was  sent  from  Charleston  to  Richmond  for  the  pur¬ 
pose  of  exchange. 

On  the  18th  of  October,  1864,  was  sent  from  Richmond  b}^  flag  of 
truce  to  Annapolis. 

During  all  of  my  imprisonment  I  have  been  treated  more  like  a 
criminal  than  a  prisoner  of  war. 

The  following  is  a  list  of  the  men  captured  with  me:  Charles  Eel- 
lick,  coxswain;  Alex.  Morring,  Robert  Armstrong,  John  Kolcbue,  John 
Hammond,  George  Boardois,  seamen;  Henry  Hockslein,  Nathan  A. 
Bailey,  ordinary  seamen;  Charles  H.  Saulsbury,  Amos  A.  Kane,  lands¬ 
men;  Edward  R.  Clark,  seaman;  and  one  man  whose  name  I  have  for¬ 
gotten,  having  lost  the  list  during  my  imprisonment. 

I  am  happy  to  report  that  I  was  promptly  obeyed  and  bravely  sup¬ 
ported  by  all  of  my  crew'. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  your  most  obedient  servant, 

Edward  L.  Haines, 

Acting  Master ,  U.  S'.  Navy. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  U.  S.  Navy ,  Washington,  1).  C.

Statement  of  First  Assistant  Engineer  Tomb,  C.  S.  Navy,  of  the  C.  S.  S.  Juno. 

C.  S.  S.  Juno, 

Charleston ,  8.  C. ,  August  8,  1863. 

The  Juno  had  a  large  spar,  with  a  65-pound  torpedo  attached,  and 
was  sent  down  on  picket  duty  below  Fort  Sumter  at  night.  We  had 
a  cotton  bale  strapped  to  the  stem,  a  few  feet  above  the  water  line,  to 
act  as  a  fender  if  we  had  a  chance  to  strike  one  of  the  enemy’s  ships. 
Lieutenant  Philip  Porcher  was  in  command;  master,  C.  Tucker;  pilot, 
William  Burk;  engineer  in  charge,  James  Id.  Tomb;  assistant  engineer, 
C.  Johnson.  We  laid  below  Fort  Sumter,  waiting,  and  had  just  started 
the  engines  ahead  when  a  large  launch  came  toward  us  and  hailed  us, 
ordering  us  to  surrender,  and  the  next  moment  tired  into  us  from  a 
12-pounder  howitzer  in  the  bow.  We  immediately  headed  for  her, 
striking  her  about  amidships;  but  not  having  much  headway  on  the 
Juno ,  the  launch  swung  around  to  port,  just  forward  of  the  wheel, 
and  then  boarded  us.  The  Juno  had  no  guns  outside  of  a  few  small 
arms.  All  the  engineer  division  with  the  balance  of  the  crew  fired 
upon  them  as  they  came  over  the  rail.  The  officer  in  charge  of  the 
launch  surrendered.  As  he  came  over  the  rail  he  had  his  sword  in  one 
hand  and  one  of  his  boots  in  the  other.  One  of  my  firemen  got  hold 
of  the  boot  and  I  ordered  him  to  return  it.  We  marched  them  all  aft 
below  as  prisoners.  At  this  time  there  were  three  or  four  floating  on 
the  port  side  swimming.  Lieutenant  Porcher  wished  to  pick  them  up, 
but  the  position  of  the  ship  was  such  we  were  afraid  to  stop  the  engines 
and  had  to  continue  into  the  harbor. 

The  next  morning,  when  taking  the  launch  over  to  the  flag-officer 
to  make  our  report,  the  officer,  an  acting  master  in  the  United  States 
Navy,  had  little  to  say;  but  the  coxswain,  who  was  seated  near  me, 
remarked  loud  enough  for  his  officers  to  hear  him:  “This  comes  from 
placing  an  officer  in  charge  of  a  boat  who  gets  you  into  trouble,  but 
can’t  get  3Tou  out,"  The  officer  said  nothing. 

James  II.  Tomb, 

First  Assistant  Engineer ,  C.  8.  Navy.

No.  66.]  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Of  Morris  Island ,  August  6 ,  1863. 

Sir:  1  have  to  inform  you  that  the  200  men  sent  by  the  Aries  have 
arrived,  but  not  having  received  your  communication  of  July  28, 
directing  her  return  to  Boston,  I  dispatched  her  in  haste  to  Hampton

I  shall  not  fail  to  employ  contrabands  when  they  can  be  had,  but  at 
this  time  nothing  is  so  scarce  here. 

The  Mahaska  has  arrived.  General  Gillmore  has  also  received  rein¬ 
forcements,  and  in  a  week  or  ten  (lays  we  shall  be  in  active  operations 
again.  Meanwhile  the  batteries  ashore  are  progressing,  and  the  ves¬ 
sels  retard  the  operations  of  the  enemy  by  daily  firing.  _ 

Major  Zeilin  has  arrived  with  260  marines,  with  which,  with  about 
the  same  number  here,  I  shall  organize  a  regiment. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  A.  Dahlgren,

Instructions  from  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  the 
organization ,  as  a  regiment ,  of  the  marines  attached  to  the  squadron. 

Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  Aug'ust  7,  1863. 

1.  The  marines  of  this  squadron  will  be  organized  as  a  regiment 
under  the  command  of  Major  Zeilin, 

2.  Who  will  indicate  to  me  the  least  number  of  marines  that  can 
execute  the  duties  of  the  several  ships  having  guards;  all  the  rest  will 
be  detailed  to  join  the  regiment. 

3.  Major  Zeilin  will  suggest  such  division  of  the  regiment  into 
companies,  and  other  details,  for  drill,  etc.,  as  may  be  necessary  for 
the  most  prompt  and  efficient  preparation  of  the  regiment  for  imme¬ 
diate  service. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


429 


4.  He  will  also  submit  from  time  to  time  requisitions  to  meet 
probable  wants. 

5.  The  dress  of  the  men  should  be  such  as  to  enable  them  to  execute 
their  duties  most  efficiently  in  this  hot  climate,  and  I  will  sanction  any 
suggestion  that  will  conduce  thereto.  The  proper  protection  of  the 
head  is  to  be  attended  to. 

6.  The  regiment  is  to  be  divested  of  all  luggage  that  can  possibly 
be  spared,  and  always  be  prepared  to  move  on  instant  notice;  rapidity 
of  movement  is  one  of  the  greatest  elements  of  military  power. 

7.  The  men  are  to  be  accustomed  to  carry  cooked  rations,  and  such 
parts  of  the  rations  will  be  supplied  as  will  be  best  adapted  to  the 
purpose. 

8.  Any  of  the  vessels  that  may  be  applied  to  will  supply  rations, 
clothes,  arms,  ammunition,  or  other  facilities  required  to  execute  the 
orders  which  maybe  given  by  me  to  this  regiment,  which  is  to  be 
entered  on  the  log  and  certified  by  the  commanding  marine  officer. 

9.  It  is  my  wish  that  the  men  shall  also  be  accustomed  to  use  charges 
of  buckshot  when  close  action  is  expected,  particularly  in  an  assault. 

10.  The  white  belts  on  dark  clothes  offer  too  good  a  mark,  their 
color  must  be  changed. 

11.  Contrabands  will  be  attached  to  the  regiment  whenever  they 
can  be  had,  so  as  to  cook  for  the  men,  pitch  and  strike  tents,  and 
perform  all  the  duties  that  can  relieve  the  marines  and  leave  them  free 
for  marching,  fighting,  etc. 

12.  There  will  be  a  detail  of  boats  from  the  vessels  of  the  squadron 
sufficient  to  land  the  regiment  conveniently.  About  half  crews  will 
be  furnished  for  these  boats. 

13.  Four  boats  will  be  selected  to  cover  their  landing,  with  complete 
crews,  in  each  of  which  will  be  a  howitzer,  with  a  crew  of  twelve 
men  and  a  field  carriage. 

J.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Gomdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore,

Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Brigadier- Gen¬ 
eral  Gillmore,  U.  S.  Army,  regarding  the  mode  of  attack  upon 
Charleston. 

Flagship  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  August  8,  1863. 
General:  I  have  just  received  yours*  marked  “Confidential,”  and 
have  directed  the  three  turret  vessels  to  be  here  on  Thursday  morn¬ 
ing.  A  large  steamer  leaves  at  once  to  tow  them. 

Last  night  it  was  my  intention  to  confer  with  you  on  the  subject 
generally  of  the  attack,  so  that  the  fire  of  the  vessels  may  be  directed 
rightly,  but  business  interfered. 

I  am  still  inclined  to  the  mode  suggested  in  a  former  letter,  but  will 
of  course  cooperate  directly  on  Sumter  if  you  wish. 

An  attack  in  front,  with  four  or  five  thousand  men  in  reserve,  can 
not  fail.  Equally  true  is  it  that  the  fall  of  Sumter  includes  Wagner. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  A.  Dahlgren, 
Rear-Admiral ,  Commanding.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  JVavy,  urging  con  immediate 
supply  of  coal,  in  view  of  the  loss  of  coal  hark  Faith. 

7o.l  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island,  August  9,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  the  Department  that  our  operations 
here  are  likely  to  be  suspended  for  want  of  coal.  I  am  just  informed 
that  the  bark  Faith,  with  500  tons  of  coal,  has  gone  ashore  and 
bilged  off  Port  Royal,  with  very  little  prospect  of  saving  much  of 
the  coal.  Besides  this,  there  has  been  but  one  arrival  here  of  coal,  a 
schooner  with  269  tons,  which  went  but  a  short  way  toward  supplying 
the  steamers.  The  Faith  was  thirty-five  days  on  the  passage. 

It  only  remains  for  me  to  urge  an  immediate  supply  by  steamers,  oi 
the  consequences  may  be  most  perplexing,  just,  too,  at  the  moment 
when  we  are  about  to  resume  active  operations. 

There  are  about  500  tons  unexpended,  including  the  arrival  above 
mentioned,  and  several  steamers  are  out. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg .  South  Atlantic  JBlockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy,  Washington,  D.  C. 


Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy,  advising,  as  a  health 
measure,  certain  additions  to  the  regular  ration. 

yrn  71  i  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

J  Off  Morris  Island,  August  9,  1863. 

Sir:  I  am  admonished  by  the  daily  recurrence  of  disability  among 
the  men  which  diminishes  their  number  rapidly,  that  some  more  than 
ordinary  measures  are  required  to  sustain  them  under  the  increasing 
labor  of  operations  in  this  enervating  climate.  Scurvy  is  now  added 


432 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


to  the  list  of  diseases,  and  to-day  the  fleet  surgeon  'recommends  the 
return  of  the  Marblehead  to  the  North,  because  to  remain  here  would 
break  down  the  whole  of  the  crew. 

I  would  therefore  respectfully  submit  to  the  Department  a  recom¬ 
mendation  to  add  certain  articles  of  diet  to  those  already  provided  by 
the  regular  ration: 

1.  Fresh  vegetables  daily,  whether  the  meat  be  fresh  or  salt;  pota- 
tatoes,  cabbage,  onions,  lemons,  etc. 

2.  A  bakery  of  fresh  bread,  for  which  some  vessel  can  be  provided 
with  a  regular  baker. 

3.  A  ration  of  ice. 

The  Department  may  be  assured  that  any  expenditure  due  to  these 
additions  will  be  amply  repaid  by  the  diminution  of  disease,  and  the 
increased  efficiency  of  those  not  yet  absolute^  reduced  to  the  sick  list. 

I  shall  make  requisitions  on  the  proper  bureau  for  the  above,  but 
also  urge  the  action  of  the  Department,  because  the  effect  of  these 
measures  has  a  general  bearing  on  our  operations. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdq.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren ,  TJ.  S.  Navy ,  requesting  the  con¬ 
struction  of  vessels  for  submarine  explosions. 

No.  76.1  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Of  Morris  Island ,  August  11,  1863. 
Sir:  I  think  the  opportunity  may  occur  where  explosions  may  be 
made  useful  under  water ;  wherefore,  1  would  ask  to  have  a  vessel 
constructed  of  corrugated  iron  (Francis),  fashioned  like  a  boat,  but 
closed  perfectly  on  the  top,  so  that  it  could  be  submerged  very  quickly  . 
There  might  be  air  vessels  at  each  end,  which,  when  exhausted,  would 
float  the  top  of  the  magazine  even  with  the  water,  when  air  was  allowed 
to  enter,  would  cause  the  vessel  to  sink. 

With  such  a  contrivance  a  quantity  of  powder  could  be  brought  to 
bear  upon  obstructions,  which  would  dislocate  any  nice  arrangements.

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Catskill ,  Commander  Rodgers ,  77.  S. 

Navy. 

August  11,  1863. — From  midnight  to  1  a.  m. :  Heavy  firing  by  the 
rebel  batteries,  answered  by  ours.  At  2:31  a.  m.  got  underway  in 
obedience  to  signal  from  flagship.  Captain  G.  W.  Rodgers  and  Pilot 
Haffards  came  on  board  and  we  proceeded  up  to  Battery  Wagner; 
went  to  quarters  and  commenced  firing  on  Wagner  at  2:46.  Expended 
6  five-second  and  3  ten-second  Xl-inch  shell.  Continued  firing  at 
Battery  Wagner  until  5:45,  when  we  ceased  and  steamed  down  toward 
the  flagship  and  anchored.  Expended  10  Xl-inch  shells  and  5  Xl-inch 
shrapnel.  Distance  from  1,000  to  1,600  yards.  At  7:45  we  and  the 
Passaic  proceeded  upon  picket  duty.  Batteries  firing  occasionally  on 
both  sides. 


Abstract  log  of  the  77.  S.  S.  Patapsco ,  Lieutenant- Commander  Badger, 

77.  S.  Navy. 

August  11,  1863. — At  4:10  a-,  m.  beat  to  quarters  and  fired  4  XV- 
inch  shells  and  1  shell  from  the  rifle  at  Gregg  and  Wagner.  Received 
1  shot  through  the  smokestack  from  Wagner.

Report  of  Commander  Reynolds ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  Senior  Officer  at  Part 
Royal ,  regarding  general  affairs. 

U.  S.  Ship  Vermont, 

Port  Royal  Harbor,  S.  C. ,  August  11,  1863. 

Sir:  I  expect  to  send  the  monitors  to  sea  to-morrow  morning,  so 
that  they  can  go  out  with  the  ebb  tide  about  9  o’clock.  The  Powhatan 
is  to  tow  one  or  two,  if  the  Cimarron  should  not  be  ready  to  take  one 
by  that  time,  and  the  Flambeau  the  Nahant.  The  Wissahickon  will 
leave  about  the  same  time  if  she  can.  It  is  supposed  she  will  be  ready 
this  evening.  The  Nahant  and  Montauk  are  coming  alongside  this 
ship  this  afternoon  to  have  the  base  rings  for  the  pilot  houses  put  on. 
The  Conemaugh  brought  up  the  Weehawken  yesterdajq  and  as  we  had 
learned  by  the  Olearider  that  the  Stettin  had  more  than  120  tons  as 
ballast,  I  have  given  the  Conemaugh  orders  to  go  down  to  the  Stettin 
and  take  coal  enough  from  her  to  enable  her  to  go  and  lay  at  Wassaw 
to  look  out  for  the  Everglade. 

A  coal  bark  has  been  signaled  as  below,  but  detained  by  health 
officer,  which  I  hope  won’t  be  long.  The  Prometheus  needs  repairs, 
which  can  not  be  made  for  some  days  yet,  and  I  am  taking  everything 
out  of  her  and  putting  it  into  Haze. 

I  will  endeavor  to  send  up  by  Haze  everything  that  has  been  written 
for  that  has  not  gone.  I  have  just  learned  accidentally  that  the  awn¬ 
ing  stanchions  for  Hinsmore ,  wrhich  wrent  by  the  Prometheus,  were  not 
taken  out  of  her.  They  will  be  put  in  the  Haze. 

All  the  coal  afloat  has  been  given  to  the  monitors,  and  the  other 
vessels  and  this  ship  have  been  helping  themselves  from  the  quarter¬ 
master’s  pile  on  Ba}^  Point,  without  which  unexpected  acquisition  we 
should  have  been  high  and  dry. 

Mr.  Danby  had  informed  me  that  b}r  keeping  the  vessels  until  Wed¬ 
nesday  evening  he  could  not  put  any  more  work  on  them,  so  I  had 
determined  to  send  them  off  Wednesda}^  morning  with  early  ebb  tide, 
but  if  I  can  get  hold  of  the  coal  bark,  I  shall  keep  them  until  afternoon, 
to  put  more  coal  into  them  {Nahant  and  Weehawken).  The  Montauk 
has  60  or  70  tons  on  board. 

The  Mercedita  went  to  sea  to-day,  having  received  orders  from  Navy 
Department  to  proceed  to  Philadelphia. 

8  p.  m.  I  have  sent  one  watch  to  coal  the  Weehawken  all  night  from 
bark  Ironsides,  so  that  she  may  leave  in  the  morning  with  the  morning 
tide. 

The  Nahant  has  just  come  alongside  for  her  base  ring  and  will  com¬ 
mence  to  coal  at  daylight.  I  shall  send  the  other  watch  to  her.  She 
will  not  get  out  till  afternoon  in  tow  of  the  Cimarron.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren ,  U.  S.  Navy ,  regarding  monitors , 
with  request  for  an  increased  number. 

No.  77.]  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island,  August  12,  1863. 

Sir:  The  communication  of  7th  August,  in  reference  to  publica¬ 
tion  of  matter  by  correspondents  in  the  squadron,  has  just  reached 
me,  and  shall  be  promptly  attended  to. 

I  do  not  know,  however,  of  any  correspondent  in  this  squadron 
except  the  editor  of  the  Baltimore  American,  who  came  to  me 
accredited  as  a  special  agent  of  the  Post-Office,  and  leave  for  passage 
from  the  Navy  Department.  Of  this  gentleman  I  have  no  reason  to 
suppose  that  he  would  commit  the  impropriety  complained  of  by  the 
Department. 

As  for  the  injury  referred  to  about  the  decks  of  monitors,  they  have 
been  easily  reparable,  and  have  not  impaired  their  immediate  efficiency 
for  battle.  The  Department  may  be  assured  that  no  effort  will  be 
wanting  on  my  part  to  derive  from  the  monitors  all  they  are  capable 
of.  Their  powers,  too,  are  carefully  husbanded,  for  the  maintaining 
of  our  own  position  inside  depends  entirely  on  these  vessels. 

I  hope  the  Department  will  reinforce  me  with  other  monitors  as 
soon  as  possible,  for  1  do  not  know  how  soon  I  may  be  in  contact  with 
Sumter  with  the  present  force,  which  is  less  than  on  a  former  occa¬ 
sion,  by  one  monitor  (at  Wassaw)  and  the  Keokuk ,  which,  though  of 
less  endurance,  was  well  fitted  for  some  work. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  veiy  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy ,  Washington,  D.  C.
