Report  of  Major  Zeilin ,  V  S.  Marine  Corps ,  regarding  the  incom¬ 
petency  of  the  battalion  under  his  command  for  the  duty  assigned. 

Headquarters  Marine  Battalion, 

Morris  Island ,  South  Carolina ,  August  13, 1863. 

Sir:  As  commanding  officer  of  this  battalion  it  is  my  duty,  how¬ 
ever  averse  to  my  inclination,  to  represent  to  you  the  state  of  this 
command.  Sufficient  sacrifice  of  life  has  already  been  made  during 
this  war,  in  unsuccessful  storming  parties,  to  make  me  anxious  at 
least  to  remove  responsibility  from  myself,  in  case  of  a  recurrence  of 
these  affairs. 

I  wish  to  state  that  the  force  of  marines,  collected  at  New  York  from 
the  various  posts,  the  receiving  and  other  ships  then  at  home,  and  now 
united  with  the  marines  of  the  South  Atlantic  Squadron  for  operation 
ashore  on  Morris  Island,  is  incompetent  to  the  duty  assigned  it.  The 
causes  of  this  incompetency  will  suggest  themselves  in  the  following: 

The  Marine  Corps  is  accustomed  to  act  in  small  detachments  on 
board  of  ship  and  ashore,  and  opportunities  rarely  offer  to  have  more 
than  one  company  together,  and  therefore  when  several  detachments 
are  united,  it  is  absolutely  necessary  that  they  should  have  time  to 
become  organized  and  drilled  as  a  battalion  and  to  know  their  officers 
and  their  duties  on  a  larger  scale.  Many  of  these  men  are  raw  recruits, 
and,  as  I  intimated,  every  garrison,  receiving  [ship],  and  even  sea¬ 
going  ships  at  the  North,  has  been  stripped  to  get  these  few  together; 
and  until  they  are  exercised  for  some  time  under  their  present  officers, 
with  whom  they  are  unacquainted,  it  would  be  very  dangerous  to 
attempt  any  hazardous  operation  requiring  coolness  and  promptness 
on  their  part;  and  no  duty  which  the}7  could  be  called  upon  to  perform 
requires  such  perfect  discipline  and  drill  as  landing  under  fire.  As 
few  of  these  have  ever  seen  an  enemy  in  any  position,  they  would 
doubtless  fall  into  great  confusion  despite  the  best  efforts  of  their  offi¬ 
cers.  All  this  was  well  known  to  the  Commandant  of  the  Marine 
Corps  when  he  was  called  upon  to  furnish,  as  he  was,  in  the  most  sud¬ 
den  manner,  and  his  opinion  was  decidedly  averse  to  risking  so  much 
with  such  material. 

Though  a  man  be  a  good  soldier  individually,  as  many  of  our  men 
are,  yet  he  must  be  accustomed  to  act  with  others  in  a  body  which  he 
knows  and  is  used  to,  before  he  can  be  relied  upon  for  any  undertak¬ 
ing  like  the  present;  but  to  expect  this  of  recruits  is  not  reasonable. 
The  officers  are  willing  to  go  cheerfully  into  any  duty  or  danger  they 
may  be  called  upon  to  face  were  there  a  chance  of  success.  They  are 
making  every  effort,  but  their  reports,  which  unite  with  the  result  of  my 
observations,  are  that  while  we  have  some  good  “  company  men,”  the 
great  majority  are  little  acquainted  with  even  company  drill,  and  all  the 
veriest  militia  as  a  battalion.  To  any  other  than  a  naval  officer  who  is 
fully  acquainted  with  the  circumstances  of  employment  of  our  arm  of 
the  service,  this  would  indeed  be  a  mortifying  acknowledgment;  but  to 
him  one  can  only  express  their  great  regret.  Blame  rests  on  no  one; 
the  exigencies  of  the  service  require  unusual  numbers  of  men;  the  old 
soldiers  are  mostly  at  sea,  and  drafts  from  shore  stations  must  be  filled 
by  new  men;  men  were  detailed  for  this  battalion  that  had  not  been 
drilled  one  week. 

Again,  few  opportunities  occur  here  for  drill,  this  morning  we 
tried  it  in  the  hot  sun  on  the  narrow  beach;  several  broke  down  and 
one  is  verv  sick.  1  had  the  drill  dismissed.  At  night  the  drill  officeis 


440 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


can  not  sufficiently  distinguish  objects  to  drill  properly;  the  small 
intervals  from  sunset  and  from  dawn  to  sunrise  onty  are  available  for 
drill;  this  time  is  too  short  and  is  necessarily  occupied  in  part  with 
other  camp  duties. 

Unaccustomed  to  living  ashore,  the  men  are  very  bad  at  caring  for 
themselves  in  cooking  and  the  various  collateral  duties  of  soldiers  in 
this  position;  hence  they  are  out  of  sorts,  sick,  and  intractable.  Hay¬ 
ing  moved  and  transferred  too  frequently,  and  separated  from  their 
baggage,  much  has  been  lost,  and  in  this  consists  yet  another  source 
of  inefficiency. 

But,  sir,  I  have  said  enough.  I  report  to  you,  my  commanding  offi¬ 
cer,  this,  the  opinion  of  myself  and  officers,  and  in  this  respect  I  deem 
my  duty  done. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  yours, 

J.  Zeilin, 

Major ,  Commanding. 

Rear-Admiral  John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Report  of  Commander  Batch ,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  a  reconnoissance 

in  the  Stono  River. 

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Pawnee, 

Stono  Inlet ,  South  Carolina ,  August  If  1863. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  all  quiet  in  these  waters. 

I  went  up  the  Stono  this  morning  in  the  Pawnee ,  the  Huron  in  com¬ 
pany,  as  far  as  Tom  Grimball’s,  but  discovered  no  new  batteries.  I 
deem  it  proper  to  report  that  we  saw  on  approaching  the  anchorage 
near  Grimball’s  three  boats,  which  pulled  up  the  river  in  the  direction 
of  Fort  Pemberton  in  great  haste.  What  their  object  could  have  been 
otherwise  than  scouting,  I  am  at  a  loss  to  know. 

We  remained  at  anchor  nearly  three  hours,  and  returned  to  our 
former  anchorage  in  Stono  Inlet. 

I  beg  leave  to  state  that  I  should  have  sent,  by  the  Oleander ,  Sur¬ 
geon  W.  T.  Hord,  who  has  been  ordered  to  the  Wabash,  but  in  view 
of  the  fact  that  we  have  a  large  sick  list,  and  furthermore,  that  1  am 
obliged  to  keep  the  Huron  up  Folly  River,  where  it  is  exceedingly 
inconvenient  to  avail  myself  of  the  services  of  the  medical  officer  of 
the  Huron,  1  have  deemed  it  proper  to  report  these  facts,  and  ask  if  I 
shall  send  Dr.  Hord  before  his  relief  arrives.  If  so,  I  shall  be  pleased  to 
learn  it  through  the  telegraph,  and  he  can  be  sent  forthwith. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  B.  Balch, 

Commander  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Rear-Admiral  John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Abstract  log  of  the  U.S.  S.  Mahaska ,  Commander  Creighton, -U.  S.  Navy. 

August  7, 1863. — Off  Charleston,  S.  C.  Occasional  firing  from  Fort 
Sumter.  At  5  p.  m.  proceeded  up  toward  Fort  Sumter;  heat  to  gen¬ 
eral  quarters  and  at  5: 15  opened  fire  on  Forts  Wagner  and  Gregg. 
Fired  32  shell  into  the  fort  but  received  no  response  from  the  enemy. 
At  6  stopped  firing  and  proceeded  down  the  bay  and  stood  out  for 
the  bar. 

August  8. — At  4:20  p.  m.  stood  up  for  Fort  Gregg,  in  company  with 
gunboats  Ottaiva  and  Marblehead.  At  4: 30  opened  fire  from  port  bat¬ 
tery  on  Forts  Wagner  and  Gregg.  The  enemy  replied  with  2  shots 
only,  the  first  passing  over  and  dropping  25  yards  astern,  second 
passed  over  and  fell  on  our  port  beam.  Two  of  our  batteries  opened 
on  Fort  Gregg,  the  latter  replying.  At  6:15  the  admiral  signaled. 
Ceased  fire  and  proceeded  down  and  crossed  the  bar;  anchored  on  the 
blockade.  Expended  98  shell  on  Fort  Gregg. 

Aiujust  13. — Firing  from  the  batteries  on  Morris  Island.  At  2:45 
p.  m.  opened  fire  on  Fort  Sumter.  After  firing  6  shot  disabled  the 
elevating  screw  of  No.  1  pivot  gun;  proceeded  to  the  flagship. 

August  If — At  11:30  a.  m.  got  underway  in  company  with  the 
Ottawa,  Wissahickon ,  and  Dai  Chung;  proceeded  toward  Fort  Sum¬ 
ter.  At  10:45  opened  fire  from  our  100-pounder  rifle  upon  Fort 
Sumter;  fired  11  shell.  The  fleet  also  fired  from  long-range  guns. 
At  11:45  the  admiral  made  signal;  ceased  firing,  and  at  12  anchored 
off  the  flagship.  From  8  to  midnight,  firing  between  our  batteries 
and  Fort  Wagner.

Letter  from  the  Secretary  of  the  Navy  to  Lear- Admiral  Dahlgren ,  U.  S. 

Navy,  agreeing  to  restrict  the  passage  of  vessels  into  blockaded  ports. 

'Navy  Department,  August  15,  1863. 

Sir:  Your  number  61  has  been  received  in  which  you  state  that  the 
British  steamer  Plover  appeared  off  Charleston  and  expressed  a  wish 
to  send  in  a  boat,  to  which  you  offered  no  objection,  and  give  your 
views  upon  the  subject  of  neutrals  passing  within  the  limits  when 
active  military  operations  are  in  progress.  _ 

I  concur  in  the  views  expressed,  and  should  deem  it  advisable  that 
no  vessel  be  permitted  to  pass  into  a  port  during  active  operations,  nor 
communication  permitted. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

Gideon  W  elles, 

Secretary  of  the  Navy. 

Rear-Admiral  Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron ,  off  Charleston. 


Order  of  Bear- Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  the  crews  of  the 
monitors  regarding  measures  for  their  comfort. 

Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island,  August  16, 1863. 

I  am  gratified  in  being  able  to  give  you  assurance  that  the  Navy 
Department  is  not  unmindful  of  your  service. 

In  reply  to  my  representations,  the  honorable  Secretary  of  the  Navy 
has  been  pleased  to  order: 

1st.  An  increase  of  25  per  cent  to  your  pay,  to  take  effect  from  the 
1st  ultimo. 

2d.  Ice  to  be  sent  for  your  use. 

3d.  A  vessel  also  to  be  sent  in  which  you  will  be  allowed  to  recruit 
when  the  service  of  the  monitors  allows. 

With  these  evidences  of  the  consideration  of  the  Navy  Department, 
I  am  sure  you  will  continue  to  do  your  duty  as  you  have  done  it, 
uncomplainingly. 

J.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

To  the  Crews  oe  the  Monitors. 


Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  readi¬ 
ness  of  the  vessels  for  action. 

No.  88.]  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island,  August  16,  1863. 
Sir:  Since  my  last  nothing  of  consequence  has  occurred. 

The  work  in  the  trenches  continues  to  progress,  and  they  were  to 
have  been  ready  to  open  fire  on  the  14th,  but  have  been  delayed  for 
a  few  days  from  various  causes.

The  vessels  are  ready  to  the  extent  of  their  power,  one  monitor 
being-  absent  at  Wassaw  and  the  Atlanta  nearly  ready  at  Port  Royal. 

Just  at  this  moment  Captain  Batch  telegraphs  from  Stono  that  the 
enemy  have  exploded  some  torpedoes  near  the  Pawnee ,  with  no  result 
save  the  loss  of  the  launch;  others  have  been  captured.  When  his 
report  reaches  me  I  shall  be  able  to  give  better  information  on  the 
subject. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  A.  Dahlgren,

Destruction  hy  a  torpedo  of  the  launch  of  the  TJ.  S.  S.  Pawnee. 

Report  of  Commander  Balch,  U.  S.  Navy. 

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Pawnee, 

Stono  Inlet ,  South  Carolina ,  August  16,  1863. 

Admiral:  A  torpedo  exploded  under  the  stern  of  the  Pawnee,  at 
midnight,  and  totally  destroyed  the  launch;  but  did  not  injure  the  ship; 
another  torpedo  went  oil'  within  30  yards  of  the  ship  at  4  a.  m.  Two 
other  torpedoes  were  captured  by  the  G.  P  Williams,  mortar  schooner. 
We  captured  a  boat  with  a  platform  for  10  torpedoes. 

1  have  but  22  tons  of  coal,  and  the  Army  has  none  here  at  present  to 
spare. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Geo.  B.  Balch,

Report  of  Commander  Balch,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Pawnee,  forwarding  draw¬ 
ings  of  torpedoes. 

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Pawnee 
Stono  Inlet,  South  Carolina ,  August  W,  1863. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor,  herewith,  to  enclose  drawings  of  tor¬ 
pedoes  which  were  sent  down  on  the  night  of  the  16th  instant  for  the 
purpose  of  blowing  up  this  ship. 

I  have  to  report  that  four  exploded  and  two  were  captured  by  the 
mortar  schooner  C.  P.  Williams,  as  reported  by  telegraph. 

I  have  one  of  them  on  board  the  Pawnee,  as  a  curiosity,  which  I 
shall  be  happy  to  send  you  if  you  desire  it. 

They  are  ingenious  and  exceedingly  simple,  and  I  respectfully  sug¬ 
gest  that  they  may  be  one  of  the  means  that  the  enemy  has  thought 
fit  to  use  in  the  desperate  attempt  to  burn  the  shipping  in  Stono,  and 
for  which,  I  learn,  volunteers  were  asked  in  a  late  Savannah  paper. 
I  trust  all  their  other  attempts  maj^  prove  no  more  successful,  though 
I  regret  much  the  loss  of  my  launch.

I  beg  leave  to  report  that  two  boats,  a  four-oared  gig  and  a  dingey,

Report  of  Commander  Balch,  U.  S.  Navy,  commending  Ordinary  Seaman  Jackson. 

U.  S.  Steam  Sloop  Pawnee, 

Stono  Inlet ,  South  Carolina ,  September  10 ,  1863. 

Admiral:  I  have  the  honor  to  transmit  the  accompanying  report* 
from  Acting  Master  S.  N.  Freeman,  commanding  the  mortar  schooner 
C.  P.  Williams ,  in  relation  to  the  bravery  and  coolness  of  John  Jack- 
son  (ordinary  seaman),  attached  to  that  vessel;  and  by  which  bravery 
and  coolness,  as  exhibited  by  John  Jackson,  I  believe  a  very  serious

August  16 ,  1863. — At  4:45  a.  m.  saw  what  appeared  to  be  two  cans 
floating  toward  us.  When  quite  near  made  them  out  to  be  two  tor¬ 
pedoes  connected  by  a  line.  Sent  a  boat  and  secured  them.  At  6  a.  m. 
hauled  them  on  shore  and  removed  the  caps,  then  towed  them  ofl‘  again 
to  the  vessel.  The  caps  were  removed  by  John  Jackson,  ordinary 
seaman,  of  this  vessel.  At  11  a.  m.  the  senior  officer  visited  the  vessel 
and  examined  the  torpedoes.  Sent  one  to  the  Pawnee  and  took  the 
other  ashore;  removed  90  pounds  of  powder  from  it  and  brought  it 
aboard  again.

SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


449 


The  Passaic  will  be  the  flagship. 

The  signal  for  movement  will  be  made  at  an  appointed  hour. 

The  monitors  with  8-inch  rifles,  Passaic  and  Patapsco ,  will  take  posi¬ 
tion  at  2,000  yards  from  Sumter. 

The  other  monitors  ( T Yeehawken,  Catskill,  Montank,  and  Nahant ) 
will  close  in  with  Wagner,  silence  its  fire,  and  then  advance  along  the 
beach  toward  Gregg,  keeping  a  fire  in  reverse  in  Wagner,  sweeping 
the  ground  north  of  it  to  Gregg,  and  if  possible  keeping  down  the  fire 
of  Gregg. 

The  Ironsides  will  assist  in  either  or  both  of  these  objects  as  circum¬ 
stances  may  dictate  in  the  judgment  of  her  commander. 

The  gunboats  having  rifles  will  take  position  about  3,800  yards  from 
Sumter,  closing  subsequently,  if  it  should  be  advisable  by  reason  of 
diminished  fire  from  Sumter  or  Wagner.  They  will  not  keep  so 
closely  together  as  to  improve  the  chances  of  the  enemy’s  fire. 

The  two  mortar  boats  will  throw  their  shells  into  Wagner  or  Sumter 
as  events  may  determine. 

In  firing  at  Wagner  it  may  be  well  to  land  the  shells  (with  long  fuzes) 
upon  the  bombproofs  or  burst  them  overhead.  The  latter  will  be  pref¬ 
erable  if  practicing  at  Sumter. 

The  flag  will  make  as  few  signals  as  possible,  still  a  vigilant  eye  is 
to  be  kept  for  such,  and  if  a  red  flag  is  shown  from  the  turret,  then 
every  effort  is  to  be  directed  by  all  upon  Sumter  unless  certain  vessels 
are  specially  designated. 

The  marine  battalion  with  boats,  howitzers,  etc.,  will  be  ready  to 
land  at  signal,  and  will  assemble  at  some  convenient  point. 

The  naval  battery  in  the  lines  will  cooperate  with  the  other  batteries 
as  may  be  requested  by  General  Gillmore. 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy. 

No.  89.]  Flag-Steamer  Dinsmore, 

Off  Morris  Island,  August  18,  1863. 
Sir:  Yesterday  was  begun  another  series  of  operations  against  the 
enemy’s  works. 

Early  in  the  morning  General  Gillmore  opened  all  his  batteries  upon 
Fort  Sumter,  firing  over  Fort  Wagner  and  the  intermediate  space. 
About  the  same  time  I  moved  up  the  entire  available  naval  force,  lead¬ 
ing  with  my  flag  in  the  Weehawken,  followed  by  the  Oatskill,  Nahant, 
and  Montauk ;  the  Passaic  and  Patapsco  in  reserve  for  Sumter;  the 
Ironsides  \\\  position  opposite  to  Wagner,  and  the  gunboats  named  in 
the  margin  at  long  range. 

Canandaigua,  Captain  3.  F.  Green. 

Mahaska,  Commander  J.  B.  Creighton. 

Cimarron,  Commander  A.  K.  Hughes. 

Ottawa,  Lieutenant- Commander  W.  D.  Whiting. 

\\  issahickon,  Lieutenant-Commander  J.  L.  Davis. 

Dai  Ching,  [Lieutenant-Commander]  J.  C.  Chaplin. 

Lodona,  [Acting  Lieutenant]  E.  Brodhead. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


453 


As  the  tide  rose,  the  Weehawken  was  closed  to  about  450  yards  of 
Wagner;  the  other  three  monitors  followed,  and  the  Ironsides  as 
near  as  her  great  draft  of  water  permitted.  After  a  steady  and  well- 
directed  hie,  Wagner  was  silenced,  about  9:20  a.  m.,  and  that  of  our 
own  vessels  was  slackened  in  consequence. 

Meanwhile,  the  tire  of  our  shore  batteries  was  working  effectually 
upon  the  gorge  of  Sumter,  which  appeared  to  have  been  strengthened 
in  every  possible  manner. 

At  this  time  the  flag  was  shifted  to  the  Passaic ,  which,  with  the 
Patapsco  (both  having  rifle  guns),  steamed  up  the  channel  until  within 
2,000  yards  of  Fort  Sumter,  when  fire  was  opened  on  the  gorge,  angle, 
and  southeast  front  of  the  work.  The  Patapsco  fired  very  well,  and  is 
believed  to  have  struck  the  southeast  front  nine  consecutive  times. 
To  all  this  Sumter 'scarcely  replied;  Wagner  was  silenced,  and  Battery 
Gregg  alone  maintained  a  deliberate  fire  at  the  Passaic  and  Patapsco. 

It  was  now  noon;  the  men  had  been  hard  at  work  from  day  break 
and  needed  rest,  so  I  withdrew  the  vessels  to  give  them  dinner.  During 
the  afternoon  our  shore  batterries  continued  the  fire  at  Sumter,  with 
little  or  no  reply  from  the  enemy,  and  I  contented  myself  with  sending 
up  the  Passaic  and  Patapsco  to  prevent  Wagner  from  repairing 
damages.  The  fort  replied  briskly,  but  in  a  brief  time  left  off  firing. 

I  am  not  able  to  state  with  exactness  the  result  of  the  day’s  work, 
but  am  well  satisfied  with  what  a  distant  view  of  Sumter  allowed  me. 
Our  entire  power  is  not  yet  developed,  as  it  will  be  daily,  while  the 
enemy  is  damaged  without  being  able  to  repair. 

The  officers  and  men  of  the  vessels  engaged  have  done  their  duty 
well,  and  will  continue  to  do  so.  All  went  well  with  us  save  one  sad 
exception— Captain  Rodgers,  my  chief  of  staff,  was  killed,  as  well  as 
Paymaster  Woodbury,  who  was  standing  near  him.  Captain  Rodgers 
had  more  than  once  asked  me  on  this  occasion  if  he  should  go  with  me 
as  usual,  or  resume  command  of  his  vessel,  the  Catskill ,  and  he 
repeated  the  query  twice  in  the  morning,  the  last  time  on  the  deck  of 
the  Weehawken ,  just  while  preparing  to  move  into  action.  In  each 
instance  I  replied,  “Do  as  you  choose.”  He  finally  said,  “Well,  I 
will  go  in  the  Catshill ,  and  the  next  time  with  you.” 

The  Weehawken  was  lying  about  1,000  yards  from  Wagner,  and  the 
Catskill ,  with  my  gallant  friend,  just  inside  of  me,  the  fire  of  the  fort 
coming  in  steadilv-  Observing  the  tide  to  have  risen  a  little,  I  directed 
the  Weehawken  to  be  carried  m  closer,  and  the  anchor  was  hardly 
weighed  when  1  noticed  that  the  Catskill  was  also  underway,  which  I 
remarked  to  Captain  Colhoun.  It  occurred  to  me  that  Captain  Rod- 
o-ers  directed  the  movement  of  the  Weehawken ,  and  was  determined  to 
be  closer  to  the  enemy,  if  possible.  My  attention  was  called  off  imme¬ 
diately  to  a  position  for  the  Weehawken ,  and  soon  after  it  was  reported 
that  the  Catskill  was  going  out  of.  action,  with  signal  flying  that  her 
captain  was  disabled.  He  had  been  killed  instantly.  . 

It  is  but  natural  that  I  should  feel  deeply  the  loss  tnussustained,  tor 
the  close  and  confidential  relation  which  the  duties  of  fleet  captain 
necessarily  occasion  impressed  me  deeply  with  the  worth  of  Captain 
Rodgers.  "  Brave,  intelligent,  and  highly  capable^ devoted  to  his  duty 
and^to  the  flag  under  which  he  passed  his  life.  The  country  can  not 
afford  to  lose  such  men .  Of  a  kind  and  generous  nature,  he  was  always 
prompt  to  give  relief  when  he  could.  I  have  directed  that  all  respect 
be  paid  to  his  remains,  and  the  country  will  not,  I  am  sure,  omit 


454 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


honor  to  the  memory  of  one  who  has  not  spared  his  life  in  her  hour  of 
trial. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Daiilgren, 

Rear- Admiral.,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Off  Morris  Island ,  August  17 ,  1863. 

At  5:30  [a.  m.]  admiral  and  staff  left  the  Dinsmore  and  went  on  board 
the  Weehawken ,  where  his  flag-  was  hoisted  at  5 :45.  Captain  Rodgers, 
chief  of  staff,  then  went  to  assume  command  of  his  old  vessel,  the  Cats¬ 
kill.  At  6:15  Weehawken  underway.  At  6:35  all  the  monitors  under¬ 
way,  standing  up  for  Wagner;  our  batteries  on  shore  firing  pretty 
briskly  both  at  Sumter  and  Wagner.  At  6:40  anchored  in  the  Wee¬ 
hawken  abreast  of  Wagner  and  about  1,000  yards  distant. 


C.  Catskill. 
M.  Montauk 


P.  Patapsco.  Ps.  Passaic. 

N.  Nantucket.  W.  Weehawken. 


About  6:45  the  Weehawken  fired  the  first  shot  at  Wagner.  At  6:49 
Wagner  replied.  At  6:50  Weehawken  fired  XY-inch  gun.  At  6:52 
the  Ironsides  opened  fire  on  Wagner.  At  6:54  Montauk  opened  fire. 
At  7  Wagner  fired  a  stand  of  grape.  Wagner  now  firing  very  rapidly 
and  using  every  conceivable  form  of  projectile  imaginable,  from  a 
Minie  ball  to  a  solid  X-inc.h  shot.  One  shot  struck  us  and  broke  in  a 
thousand  pieces.  At  7 :14  Ironsides  underway.  At  7 :15  Nahant  opened 
fire  on  rebels.  At  7 :30  Moultrie  opened  fire  and  the  shot  passed  over 
us  some  distance.  Evidently  a  rifled  gun.  At  7 :40  the  Catskill  came 
up,  anchored  just  inside  of  us,  and  at  7 :41  opened  fire  upon  Wagner. 
The  firing  from  the  batteries  on  shore  and  from  the  four  monitors  and 
Ironsides  was  now  very  heavy  and  Fort  Wagner  was  covered  by  a 
cloud  of  dust  and  smoke.  At  8:35  shifted  our  berth  nearer  in  and 
opened  again  on  Wagner,  she  firing  still;  Gregg  paying  attention 
principally  to  the  Ironsides ;  Moultrie  firing  occasional  shots,  allstrik- 
ing  beautifully  for  so  long  a  range.  One  struck  the  Ironsides  fair  on 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


455 


her  deck.  At  9:15  Catskill  moved  down  the  harbor  with  a  signal  flying, 
which,  on  account  of  the  smoke,  could  not  be  seen.  On  asking  of  the 
Patapsco  what  it  was,  she  answered  “Captain  of  Catskill  is  disabled. ” 
Could  learn  no  further  particulars.  Wagner  was  now  completely 
reduced  and  Gregg  working  but  slowly.  At  9:30  ceased  firing  from 
Weehmoken  and  got  underway  for  the  purpose  of  shifting  the  admiral’s 
flag  to  the  Passaic.  As  we  moved  down  orders  were  given  to  the  mon¬ 
itors  without  rifle  guns  to  maintain  a  slow,  effective  lire  on  Wagner 
and  keep  them  from  again  manning  the  guns.  One  of  them  had  been 
turned  over.  Wagner  silenced,  Moultrie  ceased  firing,  and  Gregg 
tiring  only  at  long  intervals. 

At  10:10  the  admiral  stepped  from  the  deck  of  the  Weehawken  to 
that  of  the  Passaic  and  his  flag  was  hoisted.  Underway  at  once  and 
standingup  the  channel,  passingthe  Ironsides ,  followed  by  the  Patapsco. 
At  10:30  Passaic  fired  from  her  rifle  at  Sumter,  extreme  elevation. 
The  shot  struck  the  fort  and  exploded  inside  and  from  the  dusty  color 
of  the  cloud  must  have  struck  the  fort  in  reverse.  At  10:35  Battery 
Gregg  opened  with  great  precision  and  energy,  the  ball  passing  but  a 
few  feet  above  our  decks  and  in  line  of  the  pilot  house.  Three  shot 
came  within  less  than  five  minutes  from  this  battery.  At  10:42  Fort 
Moultrie  opened  on  us.  Shot  striking  close  but  not  hitting.  At 
10:50-51  two  shot  struck  Passaic  from  Gregg,  one  carrying  away  the 
tripod  of  the  flagstaff  on  the  pilot  house,  the  other  striking  the  turret 
and  breaking.  The  last  one  appeared  to  be  a  cored  shot,  judging  from 
a  piece  found  on  deck.  Patapsco  also  opened  with  her  rifle  on  Sumtei 
and  struck  every  time.  At  10:51  we  fired  rifle  at  Sumter  and  XV-inch 
at  Gregg.  Firing  kept  up  by  both  Passaic  and  Patapsco  on  Sumter, 
every  shot  telling.  The  other  monitors  and  wooden  gunboats  shelling 
Wagner  and  Gregg.  At  11:15  Sumter  opened  on  us  from  her  parapet 
guns  (two)  and  in  a  short  time  firing  quite  rapidly.  At  11:05  the 
Catskill  returned  to  her  position  and  opened  again  on  Wagner.  Moul¬ 
trie  had  ceased  firing.  At  12:10  p.  in.  got  underway  and  moved  down 
to  o-ive  the  men  dinner.  Passed  within  hail  and  ordered  other  vessels 
to  go  to  dinner  also.  Learned,  when  within  hail  of  the  Catskill ,  that 
early  in  the  fight  a  shot  from  Wagner  had  struck  her  on  the  top  of 
the  pilot  house,  had  broken  the  plates,  which  were  forced  into  the  pilot 
house,  instantly  killing  Captain  G.  W.  Rodgers  and  Paymaster  J.  G. 
Woodbury  and  wounding  the  other  two  men  in  the  pilot  house.  Pas¬ 
saic  anchored  near  the  Canandaigua.  Directed  Captain  Green  to 
signal  to  the  other  gunboats  (wooden)  to  discontinue  action  and  go  to 
dinner.  The  Cimarron  was  aground  on  the  bank.  Sent  a  tug  to  her 
assistance.  At  12:30  admiral  and  staff  left  the  Passaic  and  at  12:45 
the  blue  flag  was  hoisted  at  the  main  on  the  Dinsmore.  _ 

The  wooden  gunboats  opened  about  8  o’clock,  Captain  Creighton, 
of  the  Mahaska ,  being  the  senior  officer  on  them  at  the  time,  lhe 
Canandaigua  did  not  get  inside  until  about  11:30.  1  heir  fire  was  of 

o-reat  effect.  At  4  the  Passaic  and  Patapsco  engaged  Fort  Wagner 
and  Battery  Gregg.  At  4:10  Wagner  returned  the  fire  of  the  two 
monitors.  ‘At  5:30  Ottawa,  Dai  Ching,  Wrssahickon,  LocUma,  feneca, 
Mahaska ,  went  outside  to  resume  their  stations  on  the  blockade.  At 
6-40  the  Passaic  and  Patapsco  ceased  firing  and  came  out  of  action, 
shore  batteries  firing  quite  slowly  afterwards.  5m«  went  to  1  ort 
Royal,  to  proceed  thence  to  Sapelo  to  relieve  Wamsutta  tor  repairs.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Gibson,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  TJ,  S.  S.  Seneca. 

U.  S.  Gunboat  Seneca, 

Doboy  Sound ,  Georgia ,  September  1863. 

Sir:  I  observe  in  reading-  your  published  official  report,  dated  August 
18,  1863,  of  the  general  attack  by  land  and  sea  on  Fort  Sumter,  that 
the  Seneca  is  not  mentioned  in  the  list  of  gunboats  engaged  “at  long 
range.”  1  had  returned  from  Murrell’s  Inlet  that  morning,  and  acted 
at  once  on  the  principle  that  I  could  not  err  by  joining  the  bombarding 
fleet.  I  should  have  been  engaged  among  the  earliest  had  I  not  been 
detained  by  offering  my  services  to  lead  the  way  over  the  bar  for  the 
Canandaigua ,  which  vessel  had  the  jack  flying  at  the  fore  (the  offer 
being  declined),  and  afterwards,  at  the  request  of  Captain  Green,  visit¬ 
ing  the  Dinsmore ,  to  seek  his  pilot.  I  could  not  report  to  you,  of 
course,  until  the  ironclads  were  withdrawn  from  action. 

You  will  doubtless  remember  my  chagrin,  manifested  in  conversa¬ 
tion  with  you,  at  being  ordered  off  again,  and  to  this  quiet  station,  at 
so  interesting  a  time. 

I  trust  that  I  can  not  be  wrong  in  asking,  in  behalf  of  the  officers 
and  crew  of  this  vessel,  who  are  burning  for  more  active  service,  a 
recognition  of  our  occasional  mite  in  the  reduction  of  Charleston, 
especially  on  a  day  made  sadly  memorable  to  the  service,  and  person¬ 
ally  to  myself,  by  the  loss  of  one  of  the  best  and  best-beloved  officers 
in  the  Navy. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

William  Gibson, 

Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Rear-Admiral  John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Sguadron.

Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Carpenter,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Catskill, 

transmitting  report  of  casualties. 

U.  S.  Ironclad  Catskill, 

Of  Morris  Island,  August  17,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  submit  to  you  the  following  report  of  the 
action  to-day: 

About  7:30  [a.  in.]  steamed  up  abreast  of  Fort  Wagner  and  anchored, 
Captain  Rodgers,  chief  of  stall',  in  charge;  opened  fire  on  the  works, 
which  was  returned  heavily.  About  8:30  a  shot  struck  the  top  of  the 
pilot  house,  fracturing  the  outer  plate,  and  tearing  off  an  irregular 
piece  of  the  inside  plate  of  about  one  square  foot  in  area,  and  forcing 
out  several  of  the  bolts  by  Avhich  the  two  thicknesses  are  held  together, 
pieces  of  which  struck  Captain  George  W.  Rodgers  and  Acting  Assist¬ 
ant  Paymaster  J.  G.  Woodbury,  killing  them  instantly,  also  wounding 
the  pilot,  Mr.  Penton,  and  Acting  Master’s  Mate  Truscott,  after 
which  I  hove  up  the  anchor,  steamed  down  to  the  tug  Dandelion ,  trans¬ 
ferred  them  to  her  and  returned,  taking  position  astern  of  the 
Weehawken,  continued  the  fire  until  signal  was  made  to  withdraw. 

We  were  struck  in  all  thirteen  times.  The  smoke  box  of  XV-inch 
gun  is  gradually  becoming  weaker,  the  angle  iron  around  the  bottom 
and  eight  or  ten  bolts  having  been  broken  off  to-day,  the  other  side 
being  so  badly  sprung  that  the  bolts  can  not  be  replaced.  The  inside 
bearing  of  the  after  truck  of  Xl-inch  gun  came  off  at  the  first  dis¬ 
charge,  and  was  temporarily  repaired  so  as  to  use  the  gun,  but  found 
the  axle  to  be  broken;  used  it  with  a  slide. 

Enclosed  I  send  the  report  of  Dr.  Abbott,  of  this  vessel. 

I  am,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Chas.  C.  Carpenter, 
Lieutenant-  Commander. 

Rear-Admiral  J.  A.  Daiilgren, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Commander  Parker,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  commanding  naval  battery  on  Morris  Island. 

U.  S.  Naval  Battery,  August  17,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  inform  you  that  I  lired  to-day  from  this 
battery  170  shells  and  125  solid  shot,  the  greater  portion  of  which 
struck  the  face  of  Sumter  or  its  parapet. 

By  making  officers  and  men  cover  when  shot  or  shell  were  passing 
over  the  battery,  1  avoided,  through  the  mercy  of  a  kind  Providence, 
all  casualties.  The  officers  who  were  with  me,  Lieutenant  Brower, 
Ensign  Wallace,  and  Acting  Ensign  Owens,  and  the  men,  deserve 
great  credit  for  their  laborious  exertions  of  fifteen  hours  under  a  burn¬ 
ing  sun. 

Very  respectfully, 

Foxhall  A.  Parker, 

Commander . 

Rear-Admiral  J.  A.  Dahlgren,

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  make  the  following  report  respecting  the 
injuries  received  by  this  ship  in  the  action  of  to-day. 

*Not  found.

I  count  in  all  31  hits,  though  I  think  we  were  struck*  several  times 
below  the  water  line.  The  plating  received  19  shots,  11  others  struck 
the  woodwork,  and  8  passed  through  the  smokestack.  No  matenal 
damage  was  done  to  the  armor,  though  in  four  places  the  iron  was  so 
much  crushed  in  as  to  crack  it.  The  backing,  except  in  one  place, 
where  the  width  of  the  ceiling  just  forward  of  No..  6  port  on  the  star¬ 
board  side  is  driven  in  about  three-quarters  of  an  inch,  shows  no  sign 
of  having  been  started. 

The  forward  shutter  of  No.  3  port  on  the  starboard  side  was  shot 
off  and  lost  overboard,  having  been  struck  on  its  upper  edge,  near  the 
pivot  on  which  it  swung.  One  shot  came  through  the  woodwork  on 
the  starboard  quarter  into  the  cabin  and  passed  down  into  the  ward¬ 
room,  tearing  out  a  large  piece  of  the  clamp  in  one  of  the  cabin  state¬ 
rooms,  ripping  up  the  coamings  of  the  wardroom  hatch,  and  splintering 
the  beam  underneath.  One  of  the  wheel  ropes  which  reeves  through 
the  beam  barely  escaped  being  cut  away  by  this  shot.  Another  shot 
struck  the  deck  unprotected  by  sand  bags,  just  abaft  the  partners  of 
the  mizzenmast,  going  through  the  planking  and  glancing  off  as  it  met 
the  iron  underneath.  The  iron,  however,  was  crushed  down  to  the 
depth  of  an  inch  and  a  half,  and  partially  broken.  The  deck  pump  on 
the  starboard  quarter  was  carried  away,  and  the  shot  striking  the  sand 
bags  glanced  forward  and  remained  on  deck,  but  the  knee  supporting 
the  beam  underneath  the  place  where  the  sand  bags  lay,  was  split  and 
one  of  the  carlines  broken. 

All  these  hits  were  made  by  X-inch  solid  shot  which  seemed  to  have 
been  fired  with  exceedingl}7  heavy  charges,  some  of  them  at  a  distance 
of  not  more  than  from  900  to  1,000  yards. 

Very  respectfully,  etc., 

T.  H.  Bishop, 

Carpenter. 

Captain  S.  C.  Rowan, 

Commanding  TJ.  S.  S.  New  Ironsides. 


Report  of  Lieutenant-Commander  Simpson,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Passaic. 

U.  S.  Ironclad  Steamer  Passaic, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  A  ugust  2 0 ,  1863. 

Sir:  During  the  action  of  the  forenoon  of  the  18th  instant,  when 
this  vessel,  assisted  by  the  Ironsides  and  the  Weehawken ,  was  engaged 
with  Fort  Wagner,  a  shot  from  the  enemy  (apparently  X-inch),  at  the 
distance  of  about  900  yards,  struck  the  pilot  house  of  this  vessel,  taking 
effect  at  one  of  the  peepholes. 

This  vessel  was  fitted  in  New  York,  with  the  jacket  or  sleeve  outside 
the  old  pilot  house,  and  the  space  between  the  two  was  filled  in  with 
melted  lead;  this  lead  was  squeezed  out  by  the  force  of  the  blow  of 
the  shot,  and  was  forced,  with  considerable  velocity,  into  the  pilot 
house,  inflicting  several  trifling  wounds  on  my  face  and  arm,  and 
causing  the  sleeve  of  my  coat  to  present  the  appearance  of  having  been 
peppered  with  buckshot. 

One  piece  of  lead,  in  form  a  hemisphere,  lodged  in  the  lining  of 
my  coat  sleeve,  breaking  the  skin  of  my  arm,  and  producing  a  bruise 
of  2  or  3  inches  in  diameter.

order,  without  which  I  should  not  have  made  au}^  official  mention  of

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,

General  order  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy,  annonncing  the  death  of  Captain 

George  W.  Rodgers,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Of'  Morris  Island ,  August  18 ,  1863. 

It  is  with  sincere  sorrow  that  1  announce  to  the  officers  and  men  of 
this  command  the  death  of  Captain  George  W.  Rodgers,  the  captain 
of  fleet. 

He  fell,  as  a  brave  man,  at  his  post  in  battle,  and  for  the  flag  to 
which  he  had  devoted  his  whole  life. 

Every  respect  will  be  paid  to  his  remains,  and  I  am  sure  you  will 
all  feel*  that  a  gallant  and  excellent  officer  has  been  taken  from  us, 
when  he  could  be  illy  spared. 

John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Letter  from  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy,  to  Brigadier-General  Gillmore,  U.  S,  Army, 
regarding  the  service  of  the  ironclads. 

Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  August  22,  1863. 

Sir:  The  attempt  last  night  to  batter  Sumter  was  defeated  by  one 
of  those  accidents  that  are  not  to  be  guarded  against. 

The  Passaic  grounded  far  in  advance  and  at  some  distance  from  aid. 
And  I  regret  to  sa}^  that  it  was  entirely  due  to  Mr.  Nye  refusing  to  go 
in  her  as  pilot;  some  persuasion  was  used,  but  without  effect.  lie  was 
resolute  in  his  reason. 

When  the  vessel  was  known  to  be  afloat,  much  delay  occurred,  the 
other  monitors  being  still  at  some  distance;  that  too  little  of  the  night 
was  left,  and  I  reluctantly  had  to  postpone  the  operation. 

I  just  have  your  telegram,  stating  that  the  tire  of  Wagner  is  heavy 
and  likely  to  dismount  your  guns.  You  ask  me  to  prevent  this,  which, 
of  course,  I  will  be  glad  to  do. 

It  should  be  understood,  however,  that  this  course  is  likely^  to  expend 
the  force  of  the  ironclads  so  much  as  to  render  other  active  operations 
on  my  part  impossible;  so  that  I  shall  not  be  able  to  operate  after 
Sumter  and  Wagner  are  reduced,  because  the  guns  will  be  worn  out 
and  become  dangerous,  the  men  broken  down  by  day  and  night  work, 
and  the  armor  much  battered. 

The  Ironsides  is  a  powerful  but  most  impracticable  vessel.  Her 
great  draft  prevents  approach  to  the  main  object;  at  the  same  time 
her  ports  only  allow  of  elevations  of  4  to  4£  degrees.  Then  her  ends 
are  not  armored,  and  between  Wagner,  Sumter,  and  Moultrie  she  is 
always  enfiladed  by  one  or  more  of  them. 

There  are  seven  monitors;  of  these  one  must  guard  the  enemy’s 
ironclad  at  Wassaw;  another  is  under  repair  at  Port  Royal.  Of  the 
five  here,  one  has  a  gun  disabled,  leaving  only  four  fully  available. 

Every  time  they  go  into  an  operation,  the  capacity  of  the  guns  in 
them  to  fire  is  expended,  and  probably  one-half  of  this  has  gone 
already. 

The  fire  of  Sumter  is  of  no  account.  But  most  of  the  guns  have 
been  sent  to  Moultrie,  and  I  can  not  get  near  to  one  without  equally 
approaching  the  other,  so  that  there  is  no  diminution  of  the  fire  which 
was  encountered  in  April,  but  a  great  decrease  on  our  side,  for 
Du  Pont  had  all  seven  monitors,  while  I  have  but  four  in  full  order. 

I  desire  now  to  begin  directly  on  Sumter,  but  can  not  do  so  if  the 
ironclads  are  to  be  otherwise  employed.  So  that  it  remains  to  choose 
between  this  as  well  as  further  operations  toward  Charleston  when 
Sumter  falls,  or  to  expend  power  daily  on  Wagner. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


467 


Will  it  not  be  well,  therefore,  for  us  to  agree  definitely,  which 
choice  shall  be  made;  for,  after  Sumter  is  taken,  further  progress 
will  be  arrested  if  the  monitors  are  used  up  either  in  armament  or 
otherwise. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

J.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear- Admiral ,  Oomdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Brigadier-General  Q.  A.  Gillmore, 

Commanding  Department  of  the  South. 


Order  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  TJ.  S.  Navy,  regarding  the  order  of  attack. 

Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  August  33,  1863. 

In  case  the  operation  of  last  night  is  repeated  to-night,  the  follow¬ 
ing  will  be  the  order: 

The  monitors  will  assemble  about  the  Wagner  buoy  or  Ironsides  at 
12  punctually. 

Ensign  Porter  will  place  his  boat  at  buoy  No.  3  at  midnight,  and 
when  he  sees  a  light  flashed  from  the  monitors  below  him  will  answer 
by  another  flash. 

The  monitors  will  move  together  up  the  channel  for  a  position  near 
Fort  Sumter,  following  the  Passaic  in  close  order,  and  anchor  in  a 
line  abreast,  across  the  channel,  the  Passaic  being  on  the  extreme  left. 

The  Ironsides  will  assist  as  far  as  she  possibly  can,  either  by  firing 
on  Wagner  or  in  other  ways.  The  same  signals  will  be  used  as  were 
arranged  for  the  night  of  the  21st  instant. 

J.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Corndg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron.

Report  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  U.  S.  Navy,  regarding  an  unsuccessful  night  attack 

upon  Fort  Sumter.  > 

No.  95.]  Flag-Steamer  Philadelphia, 

Off  Morris  Island ,  August  2%,  1863. 

Sir:  The  condition  of  affairs  is  of  that  nature  that  only  a  little  more 
means  are  needed  for  an  important  result. 

The  shore  batteries  have  so  ravaged  Sumter  that  if  I  had  seven  com¬ 
plete  monitors  the  work  on  it  would  be  over  in  two  or  three  days. 
But  the  cooperative  measures  that  were  required  to  bring  this  about 
have  so  drawn  on  my  means  that  I  can  not  attain  the  purpose. 

Of  seven  monitors,  one  must  guard  the  ironclad  at  Savannah,  and 
one  ( Catskili)  is  at  Port  Royal  for  repair. 

Of  the  five  here,  the  Montauk  has  a  gun  disabled.  Captain  Downes 
reports  that  the  smoke  box  just  bolds  together;  and  the  8-inch  rifle  of 
the  Patapsco  is  cracked  at  the  muzzle,  so  that  the  Passaic  and  Wee- 
liawken  are  alone  entirely  complete. 

Last  night  I  attempted  a  night  attack  on  Sumter.  It  failed  because 
the  Passaic  grounded  about  a  half  a  mile  from  Sumter,  and  by  the 
time  she  was  off  the  night  was  too  far  spent  to  get  in  position  and  do 
much  work.  Now,  1  am  hesitating  between  an  open  attack  by  day- 
light,  or  renewing  the  night  affair.  The  difficulty  by  day  is  that  most 
of  the  guns  of  Sumter  have  been  sent  to  Moultrie,  and  in  approaching 
Sumter  you  are  about  the  same  distance  from  Moultrie,  so  that  there 
are  as  many  if  not  more  guns  now  bearing  than  in  April.  Still.  I 
would  try  it  with  even  five  complete  monitors,  and  probably  will,  as 
it  is. 

Then,  the  calls  from  shore  tax  me  heavily,  for  the  trenches  can  not 
be  advanced  nor  even  the  guns  kept  in  play,  unless  the  ironclads  keep 
down  Wagner,  and  yet  in  doing  so  the  power  of  the  ironclads  is  abated 
proportionally. 

Please,  therefore,  send  me  ironclads,  if  you  have  them. 

I  have  the  honor  to  be,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Jno.  A.  Dahlgren, 

Rear-Admiral ,  Comdg.  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Hon.  Gideon  Welles, 

Secretary  of  the  Wavy ,  Washington ,  D.  C.

U.  S.  Naval  Machine  Shop, 

Port  Royal ,  S.  C. ,  August  #0,  1863. 

Sir:  In  obedience  to  your  order  we  have  examined  the  extent  of 
the  damage  done  to  the  Catskill. 

We  find  that  seven  shots  have  taken  effect  upon  the  deck,  which  will 
require  seven  plates  to  be  taken  out  and  new  ones  put  in  their  place. 

That  the  concussion  box  of  the  XV-inch  gun  was  jarred  off  from  its 
seat,  which  will  have  to  be  renewed. 

That  the  shot  which  struck  the  top  of  the  pilot  house  broke  the 
inner  plate,  which  will  have  to  be  repaired  by  putting  on  an  extra 
plate. 

The  above  repairs  can  be  done  in  eight  days. 

The  time  required  to  take  out  and  put  in  another  gun  on  the  moni¬ 
tors  will  be  four  days. 

If  the  extra  work  on  the  Catskill — such  as  the  pilot-house  sleeve, 
the  base  ring,  etc. — is  done,  it  will  require  twelve  days  additional. 

Very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Robert  Danby, 

Fleet  Engineer ,  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 

Robert  Faron, 

Superintendent  Monitor  Repairs. 

Commander  William  Reynolds, 

Senior  Officer.

Report  of  Commander  Parker,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  naval  battery  on  Morris  Island. 

Camp  Edgewood, 

Morris  Island ,  South  Carolina ,  August  83,  1863. 

Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  to  you  that,  agreeably  to  instructions 
from  General  Gillmore,  the  naval  battery  under  my  command  opened 
upon  Fort  Sumter  with  two  8-inch  Parrott  and  two  80-pounder  Whit¬ 
worth  guns  upon  the  17th  instant,  since  which  period  we  have  been 
engaged  from  daylight  to  dusk  of  each  day  up  to  the  present  time. 


472 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  whole  number  of  Parrott  shells  expended  amounts  to  703, 
of  which  373  struck  the  fort,  252  fell  short  or  went 'over  it,  and  78 
tumbled. 

From  the  Whitworth  guns  222  solid  projectiles  were  tired,  of  which 
98  hit  and  124  missed  the  fort. 

Upon  the  19th  instant  one  of  the  Whitworths  was  entirely  disabled 
by  the  reinforce  bands  starting  forward,  and  upon  the  21st  1  discon¬ 
tinued  firing  from  the  other,  as  the  slmt  were  continually  jamming  in 
the  bore,  in  ramming  home  one  of  which  four  men  were  killed  by  a 
premature  explosion  of  the  charge. 

Although  shot  and  shell  were  constantly  passing  over  and  around 
us,  through  the  mercy  of  God  they  harmed  us  not. 

The  officers  and  men  under  my  command  have  done  their  whole  duty 
to  the  country  and  to  the  Navy,  and  to-day,  as  a  reward  for  their 
labors,  have  the  proud  satisfaction  of  beholding  Fort  Sumter  a  shape¬ 
less  mass  of  ruins,  with  its  last  gun  *  dismounted  and  fallen  amid  the 
debris. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Foxhall  A.  Parker, 

Commander ,  U.  S.  Navy. 

Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren, 

Commanding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Squadron. 


Abstract  log  of  the  IT.  S.  S.  Seneca,  Commander  Gibson,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding. 

August  17 ,  1863. — From  4  to  8  a.  m. :  Our  batteries  on  Morris 
Island  and  the  whole  fleet  inside  the  bar.  Ironclads  and  gunboats  are 
in  action  with  Forts  Sumter,  Wagner,  and  Gregg.  At  10:35  a.  m. 
called  all  hands  to  quarters  for  action.  Steamed  in  and  opened  tire  on 
Forts  Wagner  and  Gregg  at  11:20  a.  m.  Expended  3  Xl-inch  shell, 
20-second  and  3  15-pound  charges.  At  12  meridian  steamed  out  of 
action,  and  at  12:20  p.  m.  came  to  anchor  near  the  flagship.  About  1 
p.  m.  half-masted  our  colors,  in  company  with  the  fleet,  for  the  death 
of  Commander  George  W.  Rodgers,  fleet  captain,  killed  on  board  the 
Catskill  in  to-day’s  action. 


Extract  from  diary  of  Rear-Admiral  Dahlgren,  TJ.  S.  Navy. 

August  15 ,  1863. — General  Gillmore  still  unwell;  also  finds  the 
quality  of  his  powder  various  and  uncertain;  asks  me  for  some,  and 
it  is  given,  of  course. 

Nothing  but  the  will  has  kept  me  up.  I  made  an  effort  to  go  ashore 
to  see  General  Gillmore.  Found  him  in  bed;  not  weakened,  however. 
He  thought  of  Monday  to  begin;  more  troops  arriving. 

August  17. — Was  a  field  day.  As  agreed  on,  the  shore  batteries 
opened  early  in  the  morning,  but  deliberately.  It  was  about  6  when 
the  monitors  began.  I,  leading  in  the  Weehaioken^  anchored  1,000 
yards  from  Wagner.  The  fort  replied.  When  the  tide  rose  I  closed 
to  450  yards,  and  about  9:30  the  fort  ceased.  The  other  monitors 
blazed  away,  the  Ironsides  and  the  gunboats  at  long  range. 


*It  was  afterwards  discovered  that  one  serviceable  gun  remained  in  the  fort. 

F.  A.  Parker. 

February  13,  1865. 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


473 


The  Catskill  had  anchored  just  on  port  bow  of  Weehawken ,  her 
length  inside,  under  Captain  G.  W.  Rodgers,  fleet  captain.  When  the 
Weehawken  was  moving  in,  I  noticed  that  the  Catskill  was  moving  too, 
and  remarked  it  to  Captain  Colhoun,  supposing  that  Rodgers  wished 
to  get  closer  than  I  was;  then  my  attention  was  taken  off,  looking  at 
the  fort,  until  it  was  reported  that  the  Catskill  was  going  out  of  action. 
Then  it  was  signaled  that  the  captain  was  disabled.  As  I  went  down 
1  heard  he  was  killed.  A  shot  striking  the  pilot  house  drove  off 
splinters  of  iron,  killed  him  and  the  paymaster,  and  wounded  the  pilot 
and  quartermaster.  When  Wagner  ceased  I  passed  to  the  Passaic  and 
steamed  up  to  2,000  yards  of  Sumter,  Patapsco  along.  Opened  on 
the  fort,  which  replied  feebly.  Our  rifle  shot  hit.  At  noon  hauled 
out  of  action. 

All  this  time  the  shore  batteries  were  doing  work,  slowly  but  surely. 

The  day  passed  over  and  the  results  looked  promising.  I  went  to 
bed  a  very  weary  man,  but  was  waked  about  midnight  by  a  telegram 
from  General  Gillmore  that  a  sortie  was  probable.  Would  the  gun¬ 
boats  stop  it? 

August  18. — Sent  up  the  Ironsides  and  two  monitors  at  early  light, 
to  keep  the  enemy  in  check. 

The  new  flagship  arrived.  I  went  on  board  in  time  to  catch  our  first 
gale.  Too  rough  to  tire. 

August  19. — Sent  the  Ironsides  to  pelt  Wagner.  General  Gillmore 
says  that  the  Whitworths  are  disabled.  Will  I  replace  them? 

In  the  evening  I  went  to  Passaic  and  steamed  up  to  look  at  Sumter. 
Pretty  well  used  up,  but  not  breached. 

August  20. — Went  into  the  creek  to  meet  General  Gillmore.  Sumter 
begins  to  show  [injuries]  under  the  continued  fire.  Ironsides  hammer¬ 
ing  Wagner.  General  Gillmore  came  on  board.  He  is  quite  satisfied 
with  the  progress. 

This  morning  the  gorge  is  beaten  in  at  the  top  and  below,  so  as  to 
make  invisible  the  arches  within. 

August  21. — The  success  of  operations  has  been  mainly  due  to  their 
being  unexpected  at  this  season.  Morris  Island  is  so  low  that  only 
the  prominent  parts  are  not  under  water  in  strong  gales.  During  the 
last  northeaster,  General  Gillmore  tells  me,  the  men  at  work  in  the 
trenches  stood  18  inches  in  the  water  and  had  to  wait  for  it  to  fall. 
Under  ordinary  circumstances  very  little  digging  shows  water.  The 
hills  of  the  south  end  (Wagner)  and  one  or  two  other  spots  alone  are 
well  above  the  sea.  No  doubt  the  Confederates  thought  we  would 
wait  for  fine  weather.  Sumter  is  now  completely  dilapidated  at  the 
gorge,  and  many  shells  have  gone  through  the  farther  walls.  So  1 
decided  to  try  a  hand  at  completing  the  work  and  assembled  the  cap¬ 
tains  of  ironclads  to  explain  my  plan.  Fixed  it,  however.  At  10:30 
were  to  move.  The  hour  came;  I  went  to  the  Weehawken;  she  had  not 
started  anchor.  Simpson  alone  understood  and  acted  rightly,  hence 
the  catastrophe. 

Just  as  I  was  abreast  of  Gregg,  “all  well,”  comes  the  scout  and  says 
the  Passaic  is  aground.  So  here  is  a  nice  mess.  No  one  knows  where. 
I  took  instant  measures,  but  so  much  time  had  been  lost  by  the  time 
she  was  off — and  I  knew  it — that  there  was  too  little  of  the  night  left. 
So  I  had  to  abandon  the  attempt.

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  New  Ironsides,  Captain  Rowan,  U.  S.  Navy. 

* 

August  17,  1863. — From  midnight  to  4  a.  m.  rebel  batteries  and  our 
batteries  continue  shelling  each  other.  From  4  to  8  a.  m. :  Light  breezes 
from  northward  and  westward,  with  passing  clouds.  At  5  gotunderway 
and  steamed  in  range  of  Fort  Wagner.  At  6  the  Weehawken  (bearing 
the  admiral’s  flag),  Passaic ,  Patapsco,  Catskill,  Nahant,  and  Montauk 
got  underway  and  steamed  in  range  of  rebel  batteries.  At  7  fired  No.  1 
gun  at  Cumming’s  Point.  Firing  starboard  battery  at  Fort  Wagner, 
with  an  occasional  shot  from  No.  1  and  No.  2  guns  at  Battery  Gregg, 
as  the  guns  would  bear.  Fort  W agner  striking  the  ship  frequently 
from  two  X-inch  guns  mounted  on  the  sea  face  of  the  battery.  Gregg 
and  Fort  Sumter  also  keeping  up  a  brisk  fire,  occasionally  striking  the 
ship.  At  daylight  our  batteries  opened  on  Fort  Sumter.  At  8  No.  3 
shutter  was  carried  away  by  a  heavy  shot  from  Fort  Wagner;  shutter 
being  struck  near  pivot,  was  broken  off  and  fell  overboard.  Firing  in 
rotation  from  Nos.  1  and  2  guns.  The  enemy  keeping  up  a  brisk  tire 
from  Batteries  Gregg,  Wagner,  and  Fort  Sumter.  At  9:30  the  enemy 
ceased  firing  from  Fort  Wagner.  At  10:15  fired  Nos.  1  and  2  guns  at 
Fort  Sumter;  shot  fell  short,  as  the  ports  would  not  admit  sufficient 
elevation.  At  10:45  opened  on  Fort  Wagner  with  port  broadsides,  as 
the  gun  would  bear.  Army  batteries  firing  on  Fort  Sumter  during  the 
watch,  enemy  replying  from  Gregg  and  James  Island.  Received  about 
30  shots,  principally  from  Fort  Wagner.  At  12:30  fired  the  starboard 
broadside  at  Fort  Wagner,  ceased  firing,  and  at  1  p.  m.  came  to  anchor, 
Fort  Sumter  bearing  per  compass  N.  W.  by  N.,  distant  3  miles;  Morris 
Island  beacon,  W.  byN.,  distant  1  mile.  During  the  action  received 
about  30  shots,  principally  from  Fort  Wagner,  of  which  14  struck  the 
plating,  starboard  side;  2  cracked  the  plate,  but  did  not  penetrate. 
Received  X-inch  shot  abaft  iron  bulkhead  on  starboard  side,  breaking 
bulkheads  and  furniture  in  cabin  and  wardroom  and  breaking  beams  and 
wheelropes;  same  shot  knocked  away  coamings  of  wardroom  hatch  on 
gun  deck.  Smokestack  badly  riddled  by  shot  and  fragments  of  shot  and 
shell  glancing  from  the  sides.  During  the  action  expended  385  Xl-inch 
shells  and  43  rifle  150-pounder  shells.  At  1:30  lowered  colors  at  half- 
mast,  Captain  George  W.  Rodgers  having  been  killed  during  the 
engagement.  At  4  the  Patapsco  and  Passaic  opened  fire  on  Cumming’s 
Point.  Rebel  batteries  and  our  army  shelling  each  other. 

August  18. — Firing  between  our  battery  and  rebel  batteries  contin¬ 
ued.  At  5:15  a.  m.  the  Passaic  and  Weehawken  got  underway  and 
steamed  up  toward  the  rebel  works  in  company  with  this  ship.  At 
8:15  a.  m.  opened  on  Fort  Wagner  with  starboard  broadside,  firing,  as 
the  guns  would  bear,  in  rotation  at  a  distance  of  1,200  to  1,400  yards. 
Passaic  and  Weehaioken  also  engaging  Fort  Wagner,  firing  slowly. 
At  9:45  ceased  firing,  having  expended  98  Xl-inch  shell  and  20  rifle 
150-pounder  shell.  Batteries  firing  on  each  other  throughout  the  day. 

August  19. — Firing  between  batteries  continues.  At  6:45  a.  m. 
flagship  made  signal  “I  wish  you  to  move  up  and  engage  Fort  Wag¬ 
ner,  firing  deliberately.”  From  meridian  to  4,  moderately  fresh  breezes 
from  northward  and  eastward  and  clear.  At  8  hove  up  starboard 
anchor  and  steamed  up  toward  Fort  Wagner.  At  9  came  to  anchor, 
Fort  Sumter  N.  W.  i  W.,  distant  3,500  yards;  Fort  Wagner  distant 
1,500  yards.  There  being  a  fresh  breeze  from  the  northward  and 
eastward,  the  ship  lay  with  her  stern  inshore  and  weather  broadside 
would  bear  on  Battery  Wagner.  Our  army  batteries  firing  on  Fort

Abstract  log-  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Montauk,  Lieutenant-Commander  Badger,  IT.  S.  Navy. 

August  17,  1863. — From  midnight  to  4  a.  m.,  the  enemy  and  oui 
forces  on  Morris  Island  kept  up  a  continuous  tiring  during  the  watch. 
At  5:20  a.  m.  got  underway  and  proceeded  to  join  the  line  of  battle. 
At  6:40  opened  tire  with  both  guns  at  Forts  Wagner  and  Gregg.  At 
7 : 20  received  a  heavy  shot  on  side  armor.  All  our  vessels  engaged 
throwing  shell  into  Forts  Wagner  and  Gregg.  The  batteries  on  shore 
actively  participating  in  same.  The  fleet  and  batteries  on  shore 
actively  engaged  shelling  the  enemy’s  works.  At  11:30  the  trunnion 
of  the  Xl-inch  gun  broke,  thereby  completely  disabling  the  same. 
Ceased  firing  and  withdrew  from  action,  having  expended  50  15-pound 
and  12  35-pound  charges  of  powder;  also  50  Xl-inch  and  12  XV-inch 
shell.  At  1  p.  m.  set  the  colors  at  half-mast  in  respect  to  the  memory 
of  Commander  George  W.  Rodgers,  fleet  captain,  killed  this  morning 
on  board  the  Gcitskill ,  while  engaging  Fort  Wagner.  From  4  to  6 
p.  m.,  firing  continued  between  our  batteries  and  the  enemy’s;  the 
Passaic  and  Patapsco  engaging  Fort  Wagner. 

August  18. — From  midnight  to  4  a.  m.  only  2  shot  fired  from  the 
enemy’s  batteries  on  James  Island.  At  7  a.  m.  the  New  Ironsides , 
Weehawken,  and  Passaic ,  as  also  the  gunboats  Lodona ,  Dai  Ching, 
Ottawa ,  WissahicJcon,  and  Mahaska  stood  in  to  engage  the  enemy’s

August  19. — From  midnight  to  4  a.m.,  occasional  firing  from  the

discovered  an  army  transport  ashore  on  the  light-house  breakers. 
At  7:30  the  Ironsides  underway,  anchoring  abreast  of  Fort  Wagner. 
Our  batteries  on  Morris  Island  opened  fire  on  Fort  Sumter  at  daylight. 
From  8  to  meridian:  Sharp  firing  from  both  our  own  and  the  enemy’s 
batteries.  At  9  Fort  Moultrie  fired  two  shot  at  the  Ironsides.  From 
8  to  midnight  occasional  firing  from  the  enemy’s  batteries  on  James 
Island. 

August  W. — At  daybreak  our  batteries  opened  fire,  which  was 
sharply  returned  by  the  enemy’s  batteries  on  James  Island.  At  10: 30 
the  New  Ironsides  and  gunboats  Lodona  and  Cimarron  stood  up  and 
engaged  the  enemy’s  batteries  on  Morris  Island.  Our  army  batteries 
actively  engaged.  At  1  p.  m.  the  enemy  opened  fire  upon  Fort  Wag¬ 
ner,  the  enemy  firing  from  James  and  Morris  islands.  From  4  to  6 
p.  m.,  the  bombardment  of  Sumter  still  continuing;  enemy  returning 
a  heavy  fire  from  James  Island.  From  8  to  midnight  the  enemv  fired 
a  few  shot  from  Forts  Wagner  and  Gregg  at  our  forces  on  i>  >rris 
Island.  At  12,  midnight,  a  strange  boat  hove  in  sight.  On  answer  to 
our  hail  replied,  “Friends  without  the  countersign.”  They  were  taken 
on  board  and  proved  to  be  deserters  from  the  Eighth  North  Carolina 
rebel  regiment  stationed  on  Sullivan’s  Island. 

August  21. — At  12:30  a.  m.  the  Ironsides  fired  two  shots,  then  sent 
up  one  rocket,  after  which  fired  several  shots.  At  12:35  discovered 
black  smoke  and  the  outlines  of  a  steamer.  Went  to  quarters,  hove  up 
anchor,  but  saw  nothing  more  of  the  steamer.  Came  to  anchor  again 
at  1 : 15  and  piped  down.  Heavy  firing  from  the  enemy’s  batteries  on 
Morris  Island  throughout  the  watch.  At  4:10  steamed  down  the 
channel  and  came  to  anchor.  Heavy  and  continuous  firing  from  our

Abstract  log  of  the  U.  S.  S.  Passaic,  Lieutenant-Commander  Simpson,  U.  S.  Navy. 

August  17,  1863. — Midnight  to  4  a.  m.,  during  the  entire  watch  our 
batteries  kept  up  a  continual  bombardment  of  the  rebel  batteries  with 
mortars,  to  which  the  rebels  did  not  reply.  Admiral  came  alongside 
and  gave  some  orders.  Montauk  and  Ironsides  steamed  up  opposite 
Battery  Wagner,  and  at  6:45  commenced  firing.  At  same  time  the 
JVahant  took  her  station  and  commenced  firing.  At  7:30  got  under¬ 
way  and  took  our  station  opposite  Battery  Wagner  and  at  7:55  com¬ 
menced  firing  XV-inch  gun  at  Wagner.  From  8  to  meridian:  At 
10:20  ceased  firing  and  retired;  the  admiral  shifted  his  flag  to  this 
ship.  Got  underway  and  stood  up  slowly  toward  Sumter.  Engaged 
Fort  Sumter  with  rifled  gun,  receiving  the  fire  of  Forts  Moultrie  and 
Sumter,  Batteries  Gregg  and  Wagner.  At  10:50  returned  the  lire  of 
Gregg  with  XV-inch  gun;  at  11:35  ceased  firing.  At  11:45  came  to 
anchor,  received  2  shots  on  turret  from  Sumter.  Fired  14  XV-inch 
shell,  9  150-pounder  Parrott  shell.  At  11.40  the  admiral  shifted  his 
flag  from  this  vessel  on  board  the  Augusta  Dinsmore.  From  meridan 
to  4  p.  m, :  At  3 : 20  p.  m.  got  underway  and  steamed  up  abreast  of  Fort 
Wagner,  800  yards  distant,  the  ironclad  Patapsco  in  company.  Com¬ 
menced  firing  XV-inch  gun  slowly  at  Fort  Wagner,  the  battery  in 
the  meantime  returning  our  fire  briskly  and  striking  our  turret  several 
times  with  great  force;  also  one  X-inch  shot  struck  our  side  armor  on 
starboard  side  amidships,  breaking  the  plating.  At  5 :45  p.  m.  ceased 
firing. 

August  18. — At  6:25  a.  m.  called  all  hands  to  quarters  and  fired 
XV-inch  gun,  to  which  the  enemy  did  not  reply;  ceased  firing.  At 
8:15  Battery  Wagner  opened  fire  at  us.  Called  all  hands  to  quarters 
and  commenced  firing  from  XV-inch  gun.  At  10:10  ceased  firing, 
having  silenced  the  fort  and  having  fired  18  times  from  XV-inch  gun. 
In  this  engagement  we  were  struck  several  times  on  the  turret.  One 
shot  struck  the  deck.

Report  of  Colonel  Keitt,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  Battery  Wagner. 

Headquarters  Battery  Wagner, 

August  17 ,  1863 — 9  p.  m. 

Captain:  I  had  the  honor  last  night  to  forward  report  up  to  1:30 
a.  m.  this  morning,  when  slow  fire  was  going  on  from  our  land  face, 
which  continued  up  to  4:  30  a.  m. 

The  enemy  responded  with  a  vigorous  mortar  fire,  ceasing  about 
the  same  time  as  ours. 

At  5  a.  m.  they  opened  a  severe  fire  of  Parrott  guns  from  their 
works  on  Morris  Island,  to  our  right,  ceasing  just  before  6.  There 
were  no  casualties  reported  from  this  fire,  and  no  material  damage 
done. 

Just  after  6  a.  m.  a  monitor  and  then  the  Ironsides  were  seen  draw¬ 
ing  up,  and  according  to  the  views  of  the  commanding  general  were 
allowed  to  come  in  close.  An  action  with  these  and  other  monitors 
commenced  about  half  past  6,  Lieutenant  Alston’s  detachment  manning 
the  two  columbiads  and  a  squad  of  Company  B,  Lucas  Battalion,  man¬ 
ning  the  rifled  32-pounder,  directed  mostly  by  Captain  [Robert]  Prin¬ 
gle  and  sometimes  by  Lieutenant  [E.  B.JColhoun.  Lieutenant  Alston 
acted  as  gunner  for  right  columbiad,  directing  his  fire  on  left  and 
nearest  monitor,  distant  about  600  yards.  Sergeant  [D.  H.]  Welch, 
Company  E,  First  Artillery,  directed*  the  fire  of  left  columbiad  against 
the  Ironsides ,  distant  about  700  to  800  yards. 

It  was  impracticable  to  train  the  right  columbiad  on  the  Ironsides. 

Captain  Pringle,  Company  B,  Lucas  Battalion,  directed  the  fire  of 
the  rifle  gun  against  the  left  and  nearest  monitor,  she  being  about  200 
yards  nearer  than  the  Ironsides ,  for  about  an  hour,  and  then  against 
another  monitor,  which  came  in  still  nearer  on  the  right,  for  about 
another  hour,  when  I  directed  the  men  to  leave  their  guns.  These 
monitors  threw  canister  and  shrapnel  frequently,  causing  great  annoy¬ 
ance  to  the  cannoneers. 

Captain  Pringle  fired  over  forty  bolts  from  his  gun,  with  little  effect 
at  first,  but  thinks  he  struck  with  one  shot  out  of  every  three  during 
the  last  two-thirds  of  his  firing.  During  this  firing,  Captain  Wampler, 
of  the  engineers,  rendered  gallant  and  effective  service  in  repairing 
traverse  circle  to  this  gun. 

After  Lieutenant  Alston  had  fired  about  five  shots  from  the  right 
columbiad,  the  monitor  came  in  so  close — within  500  yards— that&he 
was  unable  to  depress  the  gun  sufficiently  to  strike  the  turret,  though 
he  fired  some  six  shots  over  it  in  very  good  line. 

Toward  the  last  of  our  firing  (which  lasted  about  two  hours  and  ten 
minutes),  the  monitor,  which  had  been  receiving  Lieutenant  Alston’s 
fire,  drew  ofl  to  the  fleet,  apparently  injured,  and  his  fire  was  trans¬ 
ferred  to  the  next  monitor  to  the  rie-ht. 

o 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


485 


Lieutenant  Alston  fought  his  gun  all  through  our  firing,  only  inter¬ 
rupted  by  temporary  disabling  of  one  of  his  eccentric  wheels.  Ser¬ 
geant  Welch  handled  his  gun  well,  and  is  reported  to  have  struck  the 
Ironsides  several  times.  His  detachment  was  relieved,  being  worn 
out,  at  about  a  quarter  before  8,  with  detachment  from  Company  E, 
Charleston  Battalion,  under  Captain  Miles.  They  had  been  at  their 
gun  about  ten  minutes  when  a  shell  burst  among  them,  wounding  or 
stunning  every  man,  and  thus  stripping  the  gun  chamber.  Lieutenant 
Alston  had  no  men  for  it,  and,  indeed,  had  been  assisted  by  three  or 
four  men  of  Pringle’s  company. 

Captain  Miles,  being  stunned  and  very  weak,  looked  after  his 
mangled  men  in  the  hospital,  and  Lieutenant  Palmer,  Company  E, 
Charleston  Battalion,  who  had  been  assisting  Captain  Chichester  for 
an  hour,  as  adjutant,  was  soon  after  ordered  to  get  a  detachment  and 
take  charge  of  the  gun,  which  he  failed  to  do,  but  finall}'  a  detachment 
was  supplied  under  Lieutenant  [J.  W.]  Axson,  who  received  a  slight 
contusion  in  the  knee  before  the  gun  was  loaded.  They  only  firecl  it 
once,  about  8:40  a.  m.,  when,  with  the  advice  of  Captain  Chichester, 
my  chief  of  artillery,  all  the  cannoneers  on  the  sea  face  were  called  off 
to  the  passages  and  bombproofs,  as  their  exposure  was  greater  than 
any  attainable  result  would  justify.  Six  monitors  came  up,  and  cer¬ 
tainly  five  of  them  were  firing  on  this  battery  at  once,  coming  as  near 
as  they  pleased.  Various  land  batteries  of  the  enemy,  including  their 
strong  work  in  rear  of  the  stockade,  kept  up  a  brisk  fire,  but  I  do  not 
think  that  many  casualties  resulted  from  it. 

Just  before  9  a.  m.  my  acting  aid,  Lieutenant  John  D.  Hopkins, 
Company  G,  First  Georgia,  carried  an  order  to  Captain  Davenport, 
commanding  First  Georgia,  in  the  sand  hills,  to  detail  three  gun 
detachments  from  his  command,  and  led  them  up,  one  man  being 
killed  by  shrapnel  in  execution  of  this  order.  They  reported  under 
Lieutenant  [H.  A.]  Elkins  before  10  a.  m.,  too  late  to  take  part  in 
morning  fight,  and  were  put  in  charge  of  left  columbiad. 

At  9:20  parapet  in  front  of  left  columbiad  was  badly  damaged,  and 
Captain  Wampler  soon  after  took  measures  to  strengthen  it. 

Captain  Wampler  and  Major  Bryan  examined  magazines  and  reported 
them  safe.  Five  monitors  deployed  in  line. 

At  9:45  the  firing  slackened  a  "short  time,  the  monitors  drawing  off 
toward  the  south,  the  Ironsides  stationary.  At  10:15  two  monitors 
moved  to  left  of  this  battery  and  soon  a  very  heavy  fire  opened. 

Just  before  11  a.  m.  Captain  J.  M.  Wampler,  chief  engineer,  was 
killed,  while  writing  at  headquarters,  by  a  fragment  of  a  shell  cutting 
his  spine.  I  greatly  deplore  the  loss  of  this  gallant  man.  At  11:  05 
a.  m.  an  ammunition  chest  was  exploded  b}T  enemy’s  shell  at  the  field 
guns  and  some  12-pounder  shrapnel  and  shell  destroyed;  at  11:45  six 
monitors  deployed,  two  to  the  left  and  four  to  front  and  extreme 
right. 

At  12: 15  all  the  monitors,  excepting  one,  moving  to  the  south;  but 
one  drew  near  and  fired  occasionally,  and  about  half  past  12  all  firing 
ceased;  the  monitors  and  Ironsides  hauled  off  about  a  mile  to  one 
and  three-quarters.  The  men  were  turned  out  of  the  bombproof  to 
eat  and  get  fresh  air.  At  a  little  after  1  p.  m.  the  enemy  opened  a 
mortar  fire  (not  good),  which  ceased  at  2:  30  p.  m. 

At  3: 45  one  monitor  approached  battery  and  opened  fire,  soon  joined 
by  another  about  4  p.  m. ;  returned  by  our  two  columbiads  and  one 


486 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


rifled  gun.  Unfortunately  the  rifled  gun  was  spiked  in  attempting  to 
load  it,  from  the  priming  wire  having  been  carelessly5  left  in  the  vent 
and  broken  off  flush  in  trying  to  draw  it  out.  At  4: 10  a  large  hole 
was  torn  in  parapet  in  front  of  the  north  columbiad,  but  Uieutenant 
Alston  continued  fighting  it,  with  an  infantry  detail  shoveling  away 
the  sand.  Finally  the  Yates  traversing  gear  got  out  of  order. 

At  4: 40  a  XY-inch  shell  burst  under  the  chassis  of  left  columbiad,

tearing  the  platform  slightly.  Fortunately  only  one  man  of  the 
detachment  was  injured,  and  he  slightly.  They  were  from  First  (Geor¬ 
gia,  Lieutenant  Elkins  in  charge,  and  behaved  gallantly. 

4:45p.  m.:  Our  fire  ceased  about  this  time,  but  the  enemy’s  fire 
from  two  monitors  at  close  range  continued  till  nearly  6  o’clock,  since 
which  time  all  has  been  quiet. 

August  18 ,  3  a.  m. — All  quiet;  garrison  very  much  exhausted; 
repairing  damages. 

Captain  Gregorie  has  reported  as  engineer.

Additional  report  of  Colonel  Keitt,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  Battery  Wagner. 


Captain: 

*  * 


Headquarters  Battery  Wagner, 

August  18 ,  1863 — 5  p.  m. 

¥r  *■  -X*  *  * 


At  a  few  minutes  before  5  o’clock  one  monitor  moved  up  in  front  of 
the  fort,  and  opened  with  a  few  shots.  The  Ironsides,  shortly  after¬ 
wards,  and  another  monitor  followed,  taking  position  as  follows: 

The  Ironsides  nearly  abreast  the  fort,  one  monitor  a  short  distance 
to  her  left,  but  200  or  300  yards  nearer  in,  and  the  other  still  farther 
to  her  left  and  beyond  the  buoy.  Some  time  was  occupied  by  them  in 
getting  into  position,  and  at  7  o’clock  they  anchored  and  opened  fire 
sharply.  The  fire  was  replied  to  briskly  by  our  columbiad  and  rifled 
gun  for  a  half  hour,  but  was  afterwards  slackened,  in  view  of  the  short¬ 
ness  of  ammunition.  The  enemy  also  afterwards  fired  with  more  delib¬ 
eration,  and  directed  their  shots  chiefly  toward  the  rifled  gun,  which 
they  struck  with  a  shell  at  9  o’clock,  shivering  the  carriage  and  break¬ 
ing  the  trunnion  of  the  piece.  The  columbiad  continued  its  fire,  at 
intervals  of  about  ten  minutes,  until  about  11  o’clock,  when  the  fleet 
slowly  withdrew. 

The  rifled  gun  was  well  served  throughout  the  engagement,  or  until 
this  gun  was  disabled,  by  Lieutenant  Colhoun  and  his  detachment,  and 
the  columbiad  by  Lieutenant  Erwin,  who  was  very  faithful  in  the  dis¬ 
charge  of  his  duties,  continuing  at  his  post  without  relief  until  the 
fleet  had  withdrawn. 

The  monitor  against  which  our  fire  was  directed  was  struck  fairly 
not  less  than  five  times,  and  it  was  soon  after  receiving  the  last  shot 
she  moved  off,  soon  followed  by  the  other.

wind  rising,  they  all  withdrew.  Since  then  this  post  has  been  Quiet, 
though  the  enemy’s  tire  has  been  directed  all  day  against  Sumter.

Report  of  Brigadier-General  Hagood,  C.  S.  Army,  commanding  Morris  Island. 

Battery  Wagner,  August  2%,  1863. 

Captain:  Immediately  after  nightfall  on  yesterday  I  repaiied  the 
damage  done  the  VIII -inch  howitzer  on  the  salient  by  appropriating  a 
wheel  of  a  disabled  limber. 


490 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


The  enemy  fired  but  little  during  the  night;  there  was  no  firing  on 
our  side,  owing  to  the  amount  of  work  to  be  done  by  fatigue  parties, 
which  consumed  the  night. 

At  an  early  hour  two  monitors  came  abreast  of  Battery  W agner  and 
opened  fire,  which  was  kept  up  for  about  two  hours,  when  they  with¬ 
drew. 

About  an  hour  after  their  withdrawal,  the  Ironsides  took  position 
opposite  Battery  Wagner,  and  commenced  a  rapid  fire,  which  she 
continued  for  nearly  two  hours,  when  she  was  joined  by  two  monitors 
which  engaged  in  the  bombardment. 

At  2  p.  m.  they  all  withdrew.  Fire  was  opened  by  us  from  the 
VUI-inch  shell  gun  and  a  32-pounder  from  the  land  face  upon  the 
advanced  works  of  the  enemy  about  6  a.  m.,  which  was  continued  at 
short  intervals  for  one  hour  and  a  half.  We  did  not  return  the  fire 
from  the  Ironsides  and  monitors,  as  it  was  not  deemed  advisable  to 
engage  them  at  such  long  range.  The  fire  from  the  fleet,  enfilading 
the  land  face  and  proving  destructive,  compelled  us  to  cease  firing. 
As  soon  as  the  vessels  withdrew  the  sharpshooters  resumed  their 
work.

Very  respectfully  submitted. 


Johnson  Hagood, 

Br  igadier-  General ,  Commanding . 


Captain  W.  F.  Nance,

Capture  of  a  Confederate  signal  station  near  Jacksonville ,  Fla., 

August  19 ,  1863. 

Report  of  Acting  Master  Meriam,  U.  S.  Navy,  commanding  U.  S.  S.  Norwich. 

U.  S.  S.  Norwich, 

St.  John’s  River ,  Florida ,  August  20,  1863. 
Sir:  I  have  the  honor  to  report  that  while  proceeding  up  this  river 
to  Jacksonville  in  this  steamer  on  the  17th  instant  1  noticed  two  rebel 


SOUTH  ATLANTIC  BLOCKADING  SQUADRON. 


491 


signal  stations  from  which  our  approach  was  being  signaled  to  Camp 
Finegan.  I  carefully  examined  their  position  with  a  glass  and  con¬ 
cluded  they  could  be  captured  easily. 

Last  night  1  sent  an  armed  boat  expedition,  consisting  of  the  launch 
of  this  ship  and  two  cutters  of  the  Hale ,  under  the  command  of  Acting 
Master  Charles  F.  Mitchell,  my  executive  officer,  to  attempt  the  cap¬ 
ture  of  the  stations. 

They  succeeded  in  taking  one  post,  surprising  the  picket  and  com¬ 
pletely  surrounding  it  before  the  rebels  were  aware  of  their  approach. 
Owing  to  detentions  in  securing  the  prisoners,  signals,  etc.,  and  by  a 
heavy  rain  squall,  it  was  late  in  the  morning  when  they  drew  near  the 
other  station,  and  it  was  thought  best  not  to  attempt  its  capture. 

The  following  persons,  being  all  at  the  post  captured,  were  made 
prisoners: 

First  corporal  and  chief  of  post,  Charles  R.  Stone;  operator,  Wil¬ 
liam  B.  Gerry;  privates,  Thomas  J.  Wingate,  William  W.  Turner, 
and  Charles  F.  Martin. 

The  following  arms,  equipments,  etc.,  were  captured: 

Three  Enlield  rifles  with  bayonets,  belts,  pouches,  and  boxes;  16 
rounds  of  ball  cartridges  for  each  rifle;  2  signal  torches,  2  signal  flags 
(bunting),  2  spyglasses,  1  saddle. 

The  junior  officers  connected  with  the  expedition  were  Acting 
Ensigns  James  N.  Van  Boskirk  and  George  Edwards,  of  the  Hole ,  and 
Master’s  Mate  Henry  Sinclair,  of  this  ship.  Acting  Master  Mitchell 
speaks  very  highly  of  their  conduct  and  that  of  the  sailors  composing 
the  force.  The  men  from  both  ships  were  volunteers,  and  all  but  one 
of  those  from  this  ship  were  men  whose  terms  of  service  have  expired. 

The  capture  of  this  signal  station,  which  severed  their  line  within 
3  miles  of  Jacksonville,  will  either  break  up  this  end  of  the  line  or  it 
will  detain  here  to  protect  it  the  troops,  five  small  companies  (about 
200  men)  of  infantry,  two  full  companies  of  cavalry,  and  one  com¬ 
pany  of  artillery,  that  I  learn  are  about  being  forwarded  to  Richmond. 

In  closing,  I  would  mention  that  Acting  Master  Charles  F.  Mitchell 
conducted  the  expedition  in  a  manner  to  be  commended,  returning  his 
force  with  no  casualties  and  not  an  article  missing. 

I  am,  sir,  very  respectfully,  your  obedient  servant, 

Frank  B.  Meriam, 

Acting  Master,  Commanding ,  and  Senior  Officer  Present. 

Rear-Admiral  John  A.  Dahlgren, 

Comma7iding  South  Atlantic  Blockading  Sguadron.
